speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I wish to move a motion. On June 1, 1957, the people of Canada elected a Progressive Conservative government under the leadership of the late Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker. There are several members in the House of Commons and the Senate who continue to serve the House of Commons and the Senate on behalf of the people of Canada. They are the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates), the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and the hon. Senators David Walker, Orville Phillips, Robert Muir, and Heath Macquarrie. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That this House send its congratulations to these honourable Senators and Members of Parliament, wish them good health and happiness, and pray that they may continue to serve the people of Canada in the House of Commons and the Senate for many more years.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 am sure members of the House would want to express their sentiments by applauding.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CALL FOR REDUCTION OF EXCISE TAX ON NATURAL GAS TO ASSIST AGRICULTURAL INDUSTRY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the federally imposed excise tax on natural gas is putting the fertilizer manufacturing companies and the Canadian farmer at an extreme disadvantage with their American counterparts and creating a disastrous economic situation for both, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That the federal government, at the very least, drop the excise tax on natural gas to the point where both the Canadian fertilizer producing companies and the Canadian farmers can be on an equitable and competitive basis with their American counterparts.

CALL FOR REDUCTION OF TAXES AFFECTING AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the Liberal Government of Canada is supposed to be fighting inflation, and yet its own regressive taxes, for example, the excise tax on agricultural products, are inflaming inflation-this tax is approximately one third of current natural gas costs and has increased the cost of anhydrous ammonia fertilizer by as much as $93 per ton at the retail level-and the federal tax on gasoline and diesel fuel affects all farm products, which in turn increases the cost of food to the nation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Reed Deer (Mr. Towers):
That this House urges the government to be realistic and rescind the present taxes and levies affecting the farm gate prices of fertilizers, fuels, and chemicals used in agricultural production.
This will be a major step in reducing inflation.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ATTENDANCE BY CANADIANS AT UNITED NATIONS DISARMAMENT RALLY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing national necessity. During the past week five Canadian supporters of disarmament have been stopped, on orders of the U.S. government, from attending disarmament meetings connected with the U.N. Special Session on Disarmament, and

June 10, 1982
another supporter has been harassed so as to miss her booked flight, although these supporters and many others travelled freely to UNSSOD I in 1978. I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) and the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean):
That this House request the Acting Prime Minister to use his good offices with the President of the United States to persuade President Reagan to respect both his obligations as chief of state of the country that is host to the United Nations, and also the United States obligations as a signatory to the Helsinki Accords on freedom of movement, and give assurance that the thousands of Canadians planning to attend the disarmament rally this weekend at the United Nations will not be stopped, delayed, or harassed.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, whereas the traditionally unregulated deep sea shipping environment has been changing in the last decade, increasingly influenced by governments, rather than commercial forces, in support of national flag fleets; and whereas Canada relies almost entirely on foreign flag carriers to carry its vast import and export trade; pursuant to Standing Order 43, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski):
That the government be directed to bring in incentives and measures to create a climate where ship owners will be encouraged to register their vessels in Canada, receive an adequate return on their investment, and establish a Canadian Merchant Marine.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION MINISTER SEEK ADVICE FROM MAYORS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the excellent performance of Canadian mayors and municipalities which have consistently given the taxpayer the best value for money of all three levels of government while maintaining balanced budgets and a taxation level only about one third as large per capita as the federal tax levy, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid):
That the Minister of Finance be directed to seek the immediate counsel of the Canadian mayors who arc visiting in Ottawa this week, so that he might discover from them the common sense rules of competent financial management, and obtain their expert advice in preparing a new budget based on the business-like, yet practical approach which has been applied so successfully over the years by municipal levels of government.

subsubtopic: MINING LAY-OFFS AT GRANDE CACHE, ALTA.-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in view of the fact that the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) has not raised this question in his riding, I rise on the urgent matter of the lay-off of 1,170 workers in Grande Cache, Alberta, which was announced by McIntyre Mines last week. These 220 permanent lay-offs, combined with 950 temporary lay-offs to take effect on June 28, threaten not only the short-term prosperity but the longterm survival of this community, as it is totally dependent upon employment in the mines. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis):
That the Intergovernmental Mines Ministers Task Force on One Industry Towns be requested to hold public hearings in Grande Cache so that it can develop plans to ensure the economic future of one of the major towns in the riding of Yellowhead.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF NOVEMBER BUDGET-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, every day in Canada 1,185 more Canadians lose their jobs. Every day in Canada 3,500 more home owners are forced to renew their mortgages at approximately double the original rate-from 10.5 per cent to 18.5 per cent. These figures, along with all the other alarming statistics, are a direct result of the November 12,	1981, budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Therefore 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That the November 12 budget be withdrawn forthwith and replaced with a new incentive-oriented document, failing which, that this House recognize the

June 10, 1982

crisis state of our economy and therefore recommend to His Excellency the Governor General that Parliament be dissolved in order to give the people of Canada an opportunity to elect a new government which would immediately implement a policy that would put us on the road to economic recovery.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF HOMEOWNERS RENEWING MORTGAGES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in addition to the many serious economic troubles with which Canadians are forced to deal every day, the problem of mortgages continues to be a source of severe hardship. It has been estimated that up to 3,000 mortgages come due each day. Home owners who do not qualify under present programs of assistance and who have to renew their mortgages are faced with escalating rates of interest which shortly may reach the incredible level of 19 per cent. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the Minister of Finance immediately institute a further program of assistance to help this group of beleaguered home owners, a plan which would halt this cruel and unnecessary loss of homes.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR RESIGNATION OF GOVERNMENT SUPPORTERS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in a letter to The Citizen of Ottawa, the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), in her capacity as chairman of the Liberal caucus committee on economic development, stated that the Liberal caucus has responsibility to assess government policies and to offer suggestions for change. Inasmuch as by her own admission it is apparent that it is the whole Liberal caucus-and not just the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen)-which has approved government actions that have brought economic disaster to Canadians, 730 of whom are losing their jobs every day, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway):
That this House call upon decent members of government opposite to accept responsibility for their actions and resign today.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Frith) revealed in La Presse this morning that the federal government's green paper on pension reform has been postponed again, this time until the fall. The hon. member said that this latest postponement was due to "the bad economic situation". In view of the fact that it is becoming increasingly apparent that the federal government is not really serious about pension reform, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That, first, the federal government dig into the same pocket which produced $2 billion for Imperial Oil last week and bring all senior citizens at least up to the poverty line immediately, and second, since the Liberals admit they do not have the political will to include pension reform as a high priority, that they should stop pretending to the Canadian people that ensuring adequate retirement incomes are an important mandate of this government and give that job over to someone who will carry it through, namely, the NDP.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK RATE-EFFECT ON HOME OWNERS RENEWING MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who will know, of course, that the bank rate today has risen significantly, 33 points, to 16.20, which of course means that mortgage interest rates are on their way up to the record highs of last year. As this recession deepens, what advice does the minister have for the 490,000 families in this country who are facing mortgage renewals between June 1, and October 31 of this year, many of whom took out one-year mortgages last year when they were at record highs in anticipation of things getting better this year? These people will be wiped out.

June 10, 1982
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK RATE-EFFECT ON HOME OWNERS RENEWING MORTGAGES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has stated in his question that, in his view, the interest rates are on their way to the record highs of last August. 1 believe that if he has that view, it is exaggerated. I see no indication that that same record high will be achieved as a result of a significant, but nevertheless a change of 33 basis points in the bank rate which, of course, was a result of the auction held today.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN BANK RATE-EFFECT ON HOME OWNERS RENEWING MORTGAGES
speechtext: The minister's self-assurance is not very reassuring.

speakerposition: subtopic

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, can the minister go one step further and assure the House and the country that mortgage interest rates will not go beyond their present levels? They are away too high now, and he knows that. He knows that the legislation introduced in his budget is not addressing that situation.
If the minister cannot give us that assurance, and since he knows interest rates are too high already, what can he tell these half a million Canadian families who are facing economic ruin because they cannot afford to renew at these usurious mortgage interest rates or they will be wiped out? It is a very serious situation and one that 1 do not believe the Minister of Finance appreciates.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government and the Minister of Finance fully appreciate the impact of high interest rates on the Canadian people, not only home owners but farmers, small-business men, and upon investment generally. We appreciate the consequences of these rates very much, indeed. That is why all of our policies are directed against reducing the cause of high interest rates and high interest rates themselves. That is the basic solution to the problem. We have attempted, within the limits of our budget, to provide assistance to home owners who need that assistance most. We will continue to provide that kind of assistance.
I do not believe that it is within the capacity of the government to protect everyone fully against this situation of abnormally high interest rates. That is my answer to the hon. member.

speakerposition: subtopic

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister must be misinformed because he is too good a parliamentarian deliberately to mislead or even try to mislead the House. Of those in so-called dire straits whom the minister's budget was supposed to address, only 12,000 would qualify for the mortgage interest deferral. Of those 12,000, less than 1 per cent have even bothered to apply, because they know full well that if they do not hang today under that plan, they will be hung, drawn and quartered tomorrow.
If the minister holds to the view that everyone cannot be protected from high interest rates, in the name of God will he seriously try to do something for those average Canadians who are seeing their family incomes and savings and their family dreams wiped out by the attitude of this government, and by a budget that even the minister himself should be prepared to admit is in a shambles?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in a sense the hon. member spoils his own questions by putting in so many unjustified comments.

Each of these is contributing to our present situation, and none of these items has been the result of the budget of last November. The hon. member knows that, and I ask him why he does not take that into account in his questioning today.

REQUEST THAT GOVERN MENT ACT TO REDUCE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have been hearing a different tune from the Prime Minister at Versailles. He admitted that the government's efforts to wrestle inflation to the ground actually have been wrestling the economy to the ground.
We have heard from the chief executive officers of a number of chartered banks that the present high interest rates policy will devastate the economy in the next number of months. CMHC tells us that if mortgage rates go over 20 per cent, as they will because of the high interest rates, some 40,000 Canadians will lose their homes this year. Will the government
Oral Questions
consider taking the radical step of reducing the interest rate level, to enable the economic recovery to begin?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERN MENT ACT TO REDUCE INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, obviously the objective is to reduce interest rates-

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERN MENT ACT TO REDUCE INTEREST RATES

That is what we attempted to bring about through our efforts at the Versailles Summit, and that is what we are attempting to bring about through our efforts to reduce inflation. I want to assure the hon. member that if he thinks there is some easy, overnight solution to high interest rates, then he is making a mistake. If there were an easy solution I would be the first to bring it forward and implement it, but there is no easy solution.
The bringing down of interest rates requires a resolution of problems in the United States. And it requires a reduction in inflation rates in Canada, in our own country. If these two things were brought about, then I believe there would be some assurance that interest rates would drop in Canada and some relief would come to the Canadian economy.

QUERY RESPECTING REASON FOR GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the efforts of the minister to combat inflation have resulted in increased interest rates, then he should use a different approach, because interest rates have to come down. My question refers to the tactics being used now of taking more and more money out of the hands of working Canadians, a practice that we saw in the 1930s when workers were competing against other workers to get work even at less money, for fewer jobs. Can the Minister of Finance explain to the Canadian people why we are pursuing the same policy that got us into this disastrous situation as a result of the fact that the government does not know what it is doing-or is the economy totally out of control?

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Mines. A week ago we had an inventory of over 35,000 mine workers whose jobs had been affected by shutdowns, unscheduled summer vacations, and labour disruptions. This week the number is 42,000 or more. We have seen another 6,000 mine workers in the past week, and up to 200,000 mine workers and indirect service workers face unemployment because of the failure of the government to take positive and concrete steps to resolve the difficult problems within our economy.
What advice has the Minister of State for Mines offered to the cabinet? Knowing that the Government of Canada has the power to rectify this situation, what specific and concrete proposals has she made to the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister to help the thousands of mine workers who must contend with no work and countless human problems?

A number of RCAF officers taken prisoners of war while serving in Europe during World War II, contributed a part of their pay received under reciprocal agreements with the Government of Germany, to a fund to assist others in the camps who were in less fortunate circumstances. Justice and his conduct in this House. It asks that the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. As the House leader knows, this is a matter to which the government, in the British parliamentary tradition, gives time so that it can be dealt with an hopefully referred to the committee. Will the matter be given government time so that we can deal with it, or is it true that the Minister of Justice has said he does not want it dealt with and does not want it allowed any time in this House?
It is being swept under the carpet.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 checked the precedents for the kind of motion presented by the hon. member, but unfortunately, there are none at all. 1 may remind the House that the hon. member had two options, namely, to raise a question of privilege or to give forty-eight hours' notice and present a substantive motion on the subject. He preferred the first option, and he raised his question of privilege and lost. Nevertheless, he had ample opportunity during the debate on his question of privilege to try to make his point and to formulate his accusation. He had nearly a whole day to speak to this subject and express his views, and today, after losing his case, after his case was rejected and the Chair had decided there was no prima facie evidence for a question of privilege-the Chair indicated in its decision the options that were open to the opposition-he chose to take advantage of the existing procedure and to try another approach. If the hon. member had taken this option in the first place, the reaction of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), to which he referred, would probably have been different. However, first of all, the hon. member has had ample time to express his point of view which is unprecedented in this House, and as a result, we feel perfectly justified in demanding that the provisions of Standing Orders-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. 1 am not happy at all with the way the minister commented on the ruling I gave on the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). He will have to admit that my ruling was based on parliamentary procedure, and that there is no question of a member losing or having his case rejected as a result of a ruling given by the Chair. The minister may wish to explain to the hon. member at what time the motion could be considered by the House, but I would ask him not to refer to my ruling in those terms.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I may refer the hon. member to Standing Orders 15(4) and 20 which clearly establish the procedure to be followed on motions arising from private members' business. As I said before, considering the fact that the Chair ruled that this was not a prima facie case of privilege, the hon. member had ample time to express his views. He is now taking another approach open to him under the Standing Orders, and it is up to the government to decide, under the provisions of Standing Order 18(2), what the order of precedence will be. Once more, if the hon. member had not had
ample time to express his views on a previous occasion, it might be felt that to refuse to consider today's request would be inappropriate. However, the hon. member has had an opportunity to make his accusations, and secondly, and this is more important in that it distinguishes the motion from every previous precedent, the wording of the motion appearing on the Order Paper is clearly an accusation, a judgment without due process of the Minister of Justice. Anyone reading the motion will realize that it is impertinent, bold, disrespectful and unparliamentary, and never in the history of the Parliament of Canada has notice been given for a motion of this kind prior to a debate on the actual question. Because of its wording, the motion is inappropriate and unacceptable to the government, and that is why the Minister of Justice feels that he has every reason to refuse to allow any kind of precedence to be given to this motion, which is any case has already been the subject of debate.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have laid a grave charge against the Minister of Justice, namely, that he deliberately misled this House. This matter should have great priority and should be dealt with. Will the House leader give this House and a committee of this House a chance to look into the conduct of the Minister of Justice and my charge, or will the government continue to be frightened to do so and hide behind this piffle that we have just heard? I have followed exactly what the Speaker advised. This matter should be dealt with by this House and now. It is a grave charge against a minister of the Crown.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just explained that the hon. member had ample opportunity to make some noise, get publicity and plead his case earlier in this House. What 1 am saying today is that the hon. member has chosen a second way in trying to achieve his goal. He has given notice of a substantive motion which under the Standing Orders appeared on the Order Paper under private member's business.
1 think that in all fairness the hon. member is no more equal than any other member on either side of the House. Therefore, I think the hon. member for St. John's West should wait his turn. However, if the matter is so important to him even after having had the opportunity to plead his case one day and the Speaker having found that there was no prima facie case of privilege, maybe the hon. member's party would support him and move his motion on one of the three opposition days that remain in this session.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the action of the government now raises a very serious problem in procedure. As you and your predecessors have so often said, a question of privilege is rare, so rare that the House deals with a question of privilege immediately when it arises, and it should arise at the earliest
June 10, 1982

possible opportunity. That was done by the hon. member for St. John's West and the Chair dealt with that question expeditiously.
1 prefer Madam Speaker's version, your judgment on that occasion, rather than the interpretation which has been placed upon it by the government House leader. You made it quite clear that a matter of procedure was involved, as had your predecessor in the case of the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland at the time that he raised his question of privilege.
On those occasions the ongoing procedure suggested to both hon. members was that a substantive motion could be placed upon the Order Paper. There is only one reason the Chair made a suggestion like that on both those occasions, and that was to enable the House in the ordinary course to deal with the questions of privilege which were raised. In this instance, a very serious question of privilege involving a charge concerning the conduct of the Minister of Justice was repeated today in the same language which caused the Chair considerable concern on the original occasion.
The serious procedural question which arises now, if the government continues to follow this wholly undesirable course, is that we will have substantive motions of privilege languishing on the Order Paper potentially throughout the whole of a session. I am sure that is not the traditional parliamentary process.
In my submission, the government is obliged to make government time available at the earliest possible opportunity to give the House the opportunity to deal with the motion. We know that with its majority the motion itself will be defeated, but it should be disposed of and disposed of immediately. To adopt any other position or to suggest that questions of privilege should become the subject of allotted days, I really think is the kind of suggestion which the government House leader ought to reconsider seriously. Traditionally it was the government which had the obligation to deal immediately with questions of privilege and in the shortest possible time.
What it means to the Chair is this. If the government insists upon adhering to this stand, it is pointless for the Chair on future occasions which will arise even to suggest the process of putting a substantive motion down, because we now know, if the government adheres to its position, that it will never be dealt with, that it will languish on the Order Paper and indeed die with prorogation. In the meantime, the stigma is hanging over the person charged, and the question whether or not there is substance to the charge remains unanswered. Surely the illogic of that position must present itself forcefully to the government House leader.
1 have one other thing I want to say before I finish. We on this side have offered, because we know the government is hard up for time between the targets it wants to reach and now, that we would keep that debate short and indeed restrict it to only two speakers on the question. We believe strongly that the House should be given the opportunity to resolve the question, even if the government were to say to us that it will
Privilege-Mr. Andre
bring the matter on for a vote without any speakers. The government House leader made a great to do about the hon. member for St. John's West having two swings at the cat, as it were. I think there might be a disposition, even if we made no speeches, to bring the motion on, to allow the House to divide on it and to resolve the matter. It is totally unacceptable and surely totally unparliamentary to have such a substantive motion lying on the Order Paper between now and dissolution.
That is the result of the government's position, plus the other serious position in which the government House leader has placed the Chair, because no longer with any serious intent can the Chair suggest to any hon. member who raises a question of privilege that there is the option of placing a substantive motion. It will not exist if they adhere to their position.
Hear, hear!

However, the conduct of business in the House of Commons is the responsibility of the government. The Speaker has no responsibility or other obligation to rearrange the business. 1 think that is quite clear to hon. members.
Obviously this is a matter which the House leaders should negotiate between themselves and as much as possible not in the House. I have allowed this short debate or short exchange to take place because there was a question relating to government business, but I am afraid it cannot be prolonged. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise on a question of privilege of which I gave you notice earlier this day. The question arises out of a newspaper article in The Calgary Herald on Saturday, June 5, 1982. I became aware of the article on Tuesday, June 8, of this week and yesterday, June 9, would have been the first opportunity to raise the matter. But in view of the unique nature of the question, I felt I should discuss it with my colleagues and examine precedents to see how best to proceed. Subsequently I decided that the best way to proceed was to raise the matter in the House.
The newspaper article in question arose out of an interview which Your Honour had with Mr. Bob Bergen, a staff writer for The Calgary Herald. The interview occurred at the time Your Honour received an honorary degree from the University of Calgary last weekend. The article reads, in its first part, in such a manner as to suggest that Your Honour was reflecting on my actions and conduct in the House of Commons. If I might just quote from the first part of the article, it reads:

June 10, 1982
Privilege-Mr. Andre
"The rules of Parliament have to be changed to deal with radical l%0s-crn campus politics which have crept into the House of Commons," says House Speaker, Jeanne Sauve.
Sauve also said the methods of Calgary Centre MP. Ilarvie Andre, during the March bell-ringing crisis in the House of Commons typify that decade's confrontation tactics.
"In the 1960s you had campus unrest and new tactics we weren't used to", Sauve said in an interview Friday.
"Well those students are now in Parliament and they've brought with them some of their ways of expressing themselves and conducting their battles", she said.
Sauve said Andre, who engineered the bell-ringing incident in the House over the Liberal government's omnibus Energy Securities Bill, is an example of one who uses the tactics of confrontation.
"He is the one who raised the problem of the omnibus bill, quite obviously", she said.
I received from Madam Speaker's special assistant, Marie Bender, a copy of a telex she had sent to Mr. Murray Ball, news editor of The Calgary Herald, on June 7, 1982. The telex says that your Honour wished to make clear in her interview that when commenting on campus politics of the sixties your Honour made no connection whatsoever with Mr. Harvie Andre's intervention in the House; nor did you in any way convey the bell-ringing incident. The telex goes on to say:
The direct quotes in the article are correct and when one reads them against the first part of the article, they arc clearly of a general nature which is the only type of comment Madam Sauve, as Speaker of the House, would want to be associated with.
As can be seen from the quote in the article 1 read earlier to the House, the quotes attributed to you, along with the other comments in the article, clearly leave the impression that Your Honour has accused me of somehow utilizing undergraduate tactics from the 1960s in pursuit of my political objectives.

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT
speechtext: When I became aware of this article I thought I had one of three alternatives. I could have ignored the article but that would have left on the public record an apparent accusation with which I vehemently disagree.

The rabble-rousers on my left are not interested in what 1 have to say either. They can depart the chamber, then.
In the 1960s I was a professor, not a student, and if anything was on the receiving end-

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT
speechtext: That is a long time ago, Andre.

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT
speechtext: She is smiling. She thinks it is a joke.

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, perhaps if you were not smiling the jackals would not be laughing.

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT
speechtext: Show some respect.

subsubtopic: MR. ANDRE-REPORTED COMMENTS OF MADAM SPEAKER RESPECTING PARLIAMENTARY CONDUCT
speechtext:
My second course of action could have been to respond to the article by Mr. Bergen, but that would have appeared as if I were using the public media to criticize the Chair, which is something I do not feel is consistent with the conventions and practices which require that members of Parliament respect the Chair and its decisions.
My third alternative is the one 1 chose. It is to raise the matter here in the House. I have been unable to find, and I am certain there does not exist, a precedent for a Speaker to have reflected on the words or conduct of a Member of Parliament in the House or outside the House. Indeed, during the March bell-ringing incident, your Honour was very careful not to reflect on the actions of any of the parties to this dispute, and indeed such is the convention involved here. Not one of your predecessors, even though hounded by the media for reaction, would in fact have commented on the actions or conduct of any member of the House in regard to that incident. That is the strength of that particular convention.
I have had enough experience in politics to know-and have experience first-hand-that news reports do not always accurately reflect what was said or the context in which it was said. It might be that Madam Speaker was misquoted and it might be that the reporter, by taking her quotes out of context, has created a different impression. There might be other explanations.
As things stand now, this article appearing in a major newspaper in my riding, based on an interview with your Honour, clearly leaves the impression that your Honour is reflecting on my conduct as a Member of Parliament for my constituency.
I am sure that your Honour agrees with me that it would be extremely unfortunate and undesirable for this precedent situation to result in a circumstance where Speakers would be reflecting on the conduct or behaviour of Members of Parliament via the media, as it would be equally undesirable for Members of Parliament via the media, as it would be equally undesirable for Members of Parliament to be reflecting upon the behaviour of Speakers in the performance of their duties through the public media.
I feel that the matter is serious enough in terms of the unfortunate appearance that it creates that I ought to raise the matter. As I indicated, it certainly would be unsatisfactory to me, and I am sure to Your Honour, to have a circumstance where, in fact, there would be public criticism of each other via the media. I would not like to have that reflection on my conduct as a Member of Parliament remain on the public record without some correction.

1 feel a bit uneasy because the hon. member is raising a question of privilege and I happen to be the judge of that question of privilege at the same time as 1 am extremely involved in it. However, I think it would be quite clear to all members that such statements made outside the House by one member about another member do not in themselves constitute a question of privilege. Therefore, I think the hon. member would recognize with me that he does not have a basis for a question of privilege. However, if there were a basis for a question of privilege in the fact that an hon member said something about another hon. member outside the House, I think 1 would be the first one who would want to raise a question of privilege because obviously the words put indirectly in my mouth give the impression that 1 might have said things that I certainly have not said, and 1 have already told the hon. member that.
I am not misquoted because everything that is in direct quotes is exactly what I said. That appears in the latter part of the article. However, in the first part of the article there are a sequence of statements made by the reporter and allusions that I might have said that. The sequence in which these paragraphs are written gives an impression that I did in fact criticize or reflect on the conduct of the hon. member for Calgary Centre at the time of the bell-ringing crisis.
Hon. members know that I gave a few interviews during the course of that bell-ringing crisis. At that time I did not comment on anyone's actions in the House. I think that should be sufficient evidence that this Speaker knows quite definitely that there is no way the Speaker can comment on the conduct of members in the House. Certainly, 1 never did that.
Since the hon. member is quoting from the report, 1 would like to quote some of the other things which are in quotes in the article. When I read them to the House it will realize that they are hardly reconcilable with the first part of the article where 1 appeared to be reflecting on what a member might have said the reporter quoted me as saying:
The House sat down and negotiated its way out of the difficulty and that's what has to happen.
Those were my exact feelings about the crisis. In answer to another question, 1 said:
The temptation was great to do otherwise than let the House get out of its own
mess.
The reporter stated in the article:
Privilege-Mr. Andre
While Sauve says she has ideas about the nature of the reform that could take place to prevent such a crisis, she says she will only reveal them to parliamentary committees studying reform if asked.
Then I am reported to have said:
The way society now functions, and how it solves its problem by confrontation, that kind of behaviour is now reflected in Parliament.
1 did say that because 1 was being asked the question why this happens in the House in this way. If one looks around at what is happening, these tactics are admissible in some other quarters and, of course, they are reflected in the House. I certainly did not allude to the hon. member as being one of those "campus students", because 1 definitely knew that the hon. member could not possibly have been a student in 1960, and we have just learned that he was a professor.

So I think the public record has been made clear. I regret that the journalist has reported me in this way, but there is not much that I can do about it. As an experienced politician, I can assure the hon. member and give him my word that I do not think I even committed any kind of imprudence in the course of that particular interview. I am quite sure of it, I categorically state it, and I hope the hon. member will take my word, as I always take the word of hon. members in this house. (2)	To foster greater self-sufficiency of oil and gas supplies in Canada;
(3)	To promote development of oil and gas fields on Canada Lands;
(4)	To facilitate, in relation to oil and gas development, consultation and coordination with the governments of the provinces, the Yukon Territory, and the Northwest Territories;

He said: Madam Speaker, I would like to speak to this amendment, but before doing so I have some preliminary remarks that I would like to address in response to some of the comments that were made last night by the "hon. Jerry Rubin" of this House, the member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), or "radical Harv", as he is now going to be known around here! 1 never thought he was a member of the SDS; I thought it was more like the SS!
In any case, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that we heard from the Conservatives yesterday-and I see the radical member back now-speaking with respect to this bill. I really never heard such hypocrisy in all my life. How about sitting down and listening to this, because I want to quote from the letter that the hon. member has written. The hon. member from Calgary Centre, the Conservative energy critic, stood up in the House yesterday to speak on Bill C-104, a bill to give

$8.9 billion in grants to oil companies under the new National Energy Program update, and that is what the figure will be, $8.9 billion over five years. The member for Calgary Centre said he had got some changes in this bill and was quite happy. He got a judicial review of one section. He said nothing about giving $8.9 billion away. Then he criticized the petroleum incentives program grants, the PIP grants, not because they were excessive but because they were bureaucratic in filling out the forms. He should try and fill out some welfare forms or some unemployment insurance forms. He would find that they are just as bureaucratic. There is no one to defend those people, but there are many people to defend the oil companies, as the member for Calgary Centre does incessantly in this House.
Then the rest of the Conservative members got up and gave the impression that they were against this program. But here is the letter, Mr. Speaker, dated December 21, 1981. It is from "Radical Harv", the hon. member for Calgary Centre, to his fellow 1960 radical member and Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), who was also teaching university, I believe, in the 1960s. Here is what the member for Calgary Centre said:
The parts of the proposed bill dealing with the Canadian Ownership Rate and the Petroleum Incentive Program arc long overdue and we would be willing to see two relevant acts introduced and dealt with on a priority basis.
What hypocrisy for the Conservative Party to stand up and say, "We are really against this." They are not against it at all. There is the letter. What he wanted was quick dealing with it. They were saying: "Let us deal with the petroleum incentives program, let us get it over with, and let us get those grants to the oil companies as quickly as possible".
This is an incredible gift to the industry. How does the Conservative Party criticize this bill? They criticize it by saying: "Well, it may be against the Bill of Rights because it may discriminate against Canadian companies". I often think, when I hear that, of K. C. Irving sitting there in the Bahamas, the man who owns all the media in New Brunswick, the forest industry in New Brunswick, Irving Oil and a good part of other industries, including the beer industry. And we are to defend his rights as he sits there in the Bahamas!

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, 1 hope the hon. member will not want to mislead the House. Mr. K. C. Irving does not own all of the papers in New Brunswick. There are at least two or three French language newspapers that he does not own.

I am glad you pointed out that there are a couple of French newspapers. However, 1 am not here to attack K. C. Irving. I am here to deal with some of the Conservative allegations on this bill and also to deal with the bill itself. It is just incredible. We are at a time, Mr. Speaker, when the average family are having difficulties and are suffering, as we all heard from some of the questions put in question period. Yet we see this program in Bill C-104 which will give away in the petroleum incentives program more than $8.9 billion. Just think of that, $8.9 billion.

In my province the government is asking public servants and other people for restraint, not to go to the hospital because there are not enough beds, to cut back and so on. And here we are giving away $8.9 billion in grants. Think of that!
From Vancouver today, Allan Fotheringham, the Southam News columnist, writes that we should look into the salaries of some senior executives in the oil industry in this period of restraint. He quotes a report of the United States Securities Exchange Commission. That commission requires that all companies that are traded publicly disclose all facts, material or otherwise that may affect the company's business. We do not have that kind of law in Canada, so you have to go to the United States to find out the salaries of senior officials and senior executives.
According to that report, the salary of the Imperial Oil Chairman, Jack Armstrong, eased upward from $408,850 to $480,700. Poor Mr. Armstrong and Imperial Oil! The government gave Imperial Oil-I found this out in committee-$45 million to continue Cold Lake for a year. It was put on hold and Imperial just pocketed our $45 million, and Mr. Armstrong pockets $480,000 a year.
Mr. Pierce, the chairman of Ranger Oil, managed to get by with an increase from his last year's salary of $233,639 to $398,053. Is that not incredible! Just think of these large salaries and these large increases, and then think of the government in this bill giving $8.9 billion to oil companies!
The Conservatives criticize the bill because they are worried about a clause in the Charter of Rights, which they did not like in the first place. They are worried about bureaucracy in the bill. But at no time do they say that it is obscene to give $8.9 billion to an industry that says "We do not want government looking after us." If they want government to get out of their lives, let government get out of their lives. Let them do their exploration on their own, without $8.9 billion in PIP grants.
The system that we have in this country is screwy; it is upside down. Perhaps "Radical Harv" when he was a student radical in the 1960s had a different way of looking at things, but it seems to me that it is crazy, when we have so much need in medicare, in education, in job creation and so on, to give $8.9 billion to oil companies.
There will be some exploration and jobs will be created, but that will be in the north and offshore. Exploration will be done in the north by Gulf, Imperial and perhaps Dome, if Dome survives. It will be done in the Hibernia field by Mobil. Those are large American multinational companies. Have we not learned the pattern and that oil companies will want more money? Then they will go out and come back and say they have found more oil and gas, and they will want to export it, like they did one-half of their daily oil production in 1970. After they have done that, they will say there is a shortage. They will say there is a crisis, and they will come back and ask for more money. It is a never-ending circle. It is a Catch-22 situation.

1 had to sit here the other night and listen to nonsense from members of the official opposition in their attacks on the government in relation to this bill. Members of the official opposition are inconsistent. According to the Gallup poll, if an election were held tomorrow 1 suppose members of the official opposition would form the government, but it would be a government with no policy. They would give Petro-Canada away to the oil companies. They would give even more money to the oil companies. Do the Canadian people really want that? I ask the Canadian people, through you, Mr. Speaker, and through the media, to think about that. I ask the Canadian people to think about who wants to give more money to the oil companies because that is what the Conservatives have been saying.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre is the "Chicago Sevener" of this House. The other day he said in this House that he would get rid of Crown corporations, including Petro-Canada. That is his policy. That may be the policy of the blue Tories, but it is not the policy of the red Tories. Perhaps it is the policy of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) but not that of Mr. Mulroney. This is a very serious matter and the official opposition should be consistent.
There is another problem, and 1 have dealt with it in this amendment. The money provided by this bill is to be used to develop the north and offshore, but mainly in the Canadian Arctic. The government is moving out of Alberta, which is a silly policy. We should be developing the heavy oil in the Lloydminster-Wainwright area. That would provide many jobs. I received a call from Mr. Peter Susa, a representative of the steelworkers' union at the Interprovincial pipe plant at Regina. He told me that on July 14, 1982, Ipsco will lay off 516 workers for an indefinite period; 311 at Regina steel, 105 at Regina pipe, 86 at Edmonton, 80 at Port Moody and three at Brooks, Alberta. After September 30, 1982, that number will increase to 1,000. There would not be those lay-offs if the government was operating and helping in the regular industry in Alberta and Saskatchewan rather than going up to the north where American companies will be doing the basic exploration. Small Canadian contractors will not be there.
When the New Democratic Party toured Alberta, we were told at Edmonton by the ESA that its members would not be able to go up into the Canadian Arctic. They want to be close to home; that is where their jobs are.
There is another concern up in the Canadian Arctic when we go-1 was about to say "hell bent for development". Perhaps that is unparliamentary. Perhaps 1 should say "all bent for development". The problem is in relation to the native people there. They live there. It is their home, their land and their country. That is why we are introducing this amendment.
Our Motion No. 2 sets out certain objects and refers to the objects section of the Northern Pipeline Act of 1978, Section 3, which was passed by this House. The purpose of this objects section is to make clear that the petroleum incentives program must serve national and local public interests as well as provide incentives for the development of the oil and gas potential of the Canada lands. The Northwest Territories are singled out in this amendment because the other Canada lands described in Clause 2 of this bill are submarine areas, and the local public
interest is accordingly less a matter of local public debate- unless we want to include fish! There are no people there, but there are people in the north. There are native people who are the majority. There are Inuit and Dene people in the Beaufort Sea area, for example. This bill does nothing for them. It does not mention them. They were hardly even consulted about this bill. That is the Ottawa way of doing things. We put one ad in the Yellowknife newspaper to tell the people about this bill and to tell them they could come to the committee. When they came to the committee, at first they had trouble being heard but, thanks to the generosity of the members of the committee, they were able to be heard.
In passing, I want to pay tribute to the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) for his chairmanship of the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation. He did a good job.
Hear, hear!
That is the last good thing I will say about those fellows opposite.

speechtext: Now you will stop being honest.

Hon. members opposite should be putting this amendment in. The amendment deals with local participation in all aspects of oil and gas. I see the minister over there. We could continue this debate for a long time. 1 put it to the minister again that one would expect him to understand the interests and desires of a local group fighting for its rights and culture. That is what Canadian people in the north want.
We talked about the issues of the sixties, and I made fun of the hon. member for Calgary Centre. I said he was the Jerry Rubin of this House. One of the issues in the United States in the sixties was the treatment of minority groups, especially black people, with some dignity. The Americans passed a number of civil rights acts. We have never faced up to that in Canada. We have a problem in Canada. We like to talk about how bad South Africa, the United States and other places are, but the way we treat our native people in this country is shameful and we have to change. This House is the place to change. The native people are the majority in the north. This bill deals with giving grants for speeding up exploration in the north, especially in the Beaufort Sea area and the western Arctic, but what do we do about consulting local people? Nothing. This amendment simply says that as part of the statement of objects in this bill, we should try to maximize economic benefits to the people who are there. The amendment reads:
-at the same time minimizing any adverse effect on the social and environmental conditions of the areas most directly affected-
A native chief, Sam Raddi, told a federal government inquiry that there is a story the native people tell. His father told him and his father's father told his father. The story is passed down through the generations. The story is that if the animals ever disappear from the Beaufort Sea area-the cariboo, the whale and the seal-then the people go next.
June 10, 1982

There is much we could learn from native people. We could gain much wisdom about life from them. If we do not look after our environment, we will disappear because we are part of that environment. That is what we have to learn.
That is why we have introduced a clause like this. It talks about local participation in oil and gas development. It does not require the government to do anything in terms of levying tax. The Crown does not have to spend money. All the amendment says is that the government must consider local development. It must consider the native people and the people who call that area their home. Most Canadians live in the south of Canada along a strip right across the country which is near the United States. Some people still think about the north. There is good will in southern Canada for the north-even in Toronto-because Canadians are a northern people. When we deal with the north in any of these bills we should not forget the people there. I think in southern Canada there is support for northern interests.
All we ask is that the government adopt this amendment which will give firm protection to the north and will show some concern for the native people who call the north their home.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in support of Motion No. 2 introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) and to express my appreciation for the job he has done in raising what I consider the real issues of this whole energy package.
Our concern with this bill is that it proposes a massive incentive program for the oil companies without any guaranteed benefits for the Canadian people. The idea of an incentive is to give some person or some organization a reason for taking action. By making provision for the payment of some $8.9 billion to the oil companies, the government is giving them plenty of reason to act but is rather vague about the actions it requires from them, other than simply that they should spend money on petroleum exploration and development of the Canada lands.
The bill sets out the framework for paying $8.9 billion of taxpayers' money to the oil companies so that the federal government can do an end run around the petroleum producing provinces.
In Hamlet there is an interesting situation in which Hamlet, sitting by the graveside, considers the whole cycle of human mortality-how a person can die and rot and become earth that in turn nurtures food that goes into other human beings. Then he says that in this way a king can do a progress through the guts of a beggar. Under PIP, the money of poor people paid out in taxes does a progress through the guts of the bureaucracy and ends up in the pockets of the oil companies.
This amendment sets out the objects which we believe the act should achieve. If we are to have incentives, then they should be directed toward goals that are in accord with our
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
national purpose. Simply shovelling money out to the companies may be a well-established Canadian custom but it hardly constitutes a national goal around which all Canadians of intelligence and good will can unite.
The amendment sets out some objectives which should be an integral part of any incentive program. Some of these objectives have been overlooked. The amendment states, in part, as follows:
The objects of this Act are:
(1) To provide a petroleum incentive program;
There is no question about that, Mr. Speaker. Providing $8.9 billion to the oil companies will give them plenty of incentive. The remaining five objectives set out the benefits that should accrue to Canadians as a result of this $8.9 billion. Let us consider the merits of these objectives and ask how well the bill measures up to them. Does the bill promote these objectives as well as it promotes giving money to the oil companies? The second objective reads:
To foster greater self-sufficiency of oil and gas supplies in Canada;
The question of self-sufficiency in oil and gas has been at the centre of Canadian political debate for the last decade. All parties agree that energy self-sufficiency is a desirable objective. Certainly it is one of the standards against which PIP should be measured.
We have serious questions about whether $8.9 billion for the oil companies is the way to achieve self-sufficiency. That $8.9 billion could be used in ways to achieve much more, such as enhanced recovery, an increased program of conservation and putting money into alternate energy. If we consider some of the situations in which we are involved we find, for example, that Dome, in exchange for Japanese financing, has already promised to export petroleum resources from the Beaufort. We have to ask how increased exports will lead to greater selfsufficiency. We know very well that it will not. We travelled this route ten or fifteen years ago and that is why we are facing the present crisis.
The third objective is:
To promote development of oil and gas fields on Canada lands.
The act will indeed do this by providing up to 80 per cent of drilling and exploration costs. This is one of the objectives of the act and it should be stated as such. We have to ask how desirable this goal is. Is it to the advantage of Canadians to pay $8.9 billion for a program that ignores more accessible petroleum reserves in the western provinces? Is drilling in the Beaufort Sea, with all the attendant environmental risks, the best way to achieve energy security in Canada? We have to ask if it is in our own best interests as a nation to encourage the economic equivalent of a pre-emptive strike on land that is still subject to land claims negotiations. Is it really part of our national character to deal craftily with the aboriginal people of the north, guaranteeing them aboriginal rights in the Constitution but eroding those rights and circumscribing them by this legislation which gives out incentives for development on lands for which claims are under negotiation?

Petroleum Incentives Program Act
The fourth objective is this:
To facilitate, in relation to oil and gas development, consultation and coordination with the governments of the provinces, the Yukon Territory, and the Northwest Territories;
Canada is a federal state and co-operation should be the hallmark of any energy legislation. Where the government was unable to get along with the producing provinces which have a degree of sovereignty in their own sphere, it simply picked up its marbles and headed for the territories where it hopes it can still reign supreme. No consultation with the territories has taken place. No revenue-sharing agreement has been reached with them. Instead, the territories will be completely dependent upon the largesse and generosity of the federal government-as the 13 American colonies were dependent upon George III. The government seems to be about as stupid and insensitive as George III. Perhaps it should look at history to see what happened there.
The people of the north are tired of exploitation without consultation. They object to the imposition of a form of development that denies their basic right to determine their own future. There is a need to return to co-operative federalism and to include the territories.
The fifth objective reads:
To maximize the social and economic benefits from the oil and gas developments on Canada Lands, including the maximizing of the opportunities for employment of Canadians while at the same time minimizing any adverse effect on the social and environmental conditions of the areas most directly affected by the oil and gas developments;
The question "What's in it for me?" may not be satisfactory as a total human philosophy, but it is a pretty important question for most Canadians today. We know that each of us will have to pay a pretty hefty chunk of that $8.9 billion, at a time when we have trouble raising money for housing, for health care and for higher education. It is important that we ask what are we getting for it in the way of jobs, and how many. Will there be enough for my kids coming out of school, where will they be, how long will they last and how much will they pay? With two million Canadians out of work these are not frivolous questions. Unfortunately, while this should be an objective of the incentive program, there is nothing in the bill which says how it would meet this objective. There are no guarantees, the incentives are only for exploration and development, and there is no requirement for performance in terms of job creation.
The second part of this objective talks about minimizing adverse effects on the people most affected. We have to recognize that oil drilling and exploration in the north will mean major disruption in the lifestyle of northern people. Unfortunately there is nothing in this incentive program which even asks the companies to raise that as a concern. The record of the government is one of dragging its feet on land claims negotiations and cutting back on money for environmental grants.
I am pleased to see the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) is here today and I would be interested in hearing his comments on the fact that the Beaufort Sea coalition has had its grants cut back by some 62 per cent. How are we going to be concerned about the environment at the same time as we are cutting back on the money? There was a promise of $10 million to help the people of the north deal with the social impact of the Norman Wells pipeline, but none of it has materialized. It is important that this bill recognizes as an objective the need to maximize the benefits and minimize the adverse effects; then we can measure the program to see how well it delivers.
The final objective is:
To advance national economic and energy interests and local public interest in social and economic development by ensuring the highest possible degree of Canadian participation in general, and local participation in particular, in all aspects of the oil and gas development in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
Basically we want guarantees to the highest possible extent of Canadian and local participation. The people who suffer the adverse effects should get some of the benefits. But the bill does not do that.
When we were debating Bill C-48 last year and looking at its basic philosophy, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way pointed out time and again that the numbers regarding Canadian ownership could be and would be fiddled. If we look at the first major contract given out under that bill, we see that Esso, with about 30 per cent Canadian ownership, has formed some kind of a paper consortium involving ten other companies so that it will have some kind of Canadian content and be able to get the money from the Canadian people.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, does not really achieve the goals it should. I think we should at least have a statement of our objectives, and we can then see whether or not it measures up. Therefore, I urge the adoption of this amendment.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the PIP grants is to promote greater private Canadian ownership in the industry. The higher the Canadian ownership rate, COR, the greater the grant. When the NEP was first introduced in 1980, presumably after much consideration and determination by cabinet- although I wonder-they agreed to push ahead with Canadi-anization as rapidly as possible. The COR levels were in three categories: zero to 50 per cent; 50 per cent to 75 per cent; over 75 per cent. Because of intense lobbying by the industry, including Conservative members, the COR levels have been reduced and an intermediate category has been added.
The effect of this amendment will be to institute a 50 per cent to 64 per cent COR for level 2 beginning in 1981, a 65 per cent to 74 per cent COR for level 3 beginning in, 1981, and a 75 per cent plus COR for level 4 beginning in 1981, instead of phasing in percentage levels as presently in the bill.
The Liberals, Mr. Speaker, have decided to Canadianize. You know their motto very well: "Don't do anything by half that you can do by quarters." This bill is an example of that. Canadianization is not a yacht race, you do not have to tack and weave and so on. It seems to me that if you have a goal, you approach the goal.
We in the NDP would not Canadianize in this way. It is unworkable, bureaucratic, and a big giveaway to Imperial Oil and its friends. But this is the way the government has chosen to Canadianize. It seems to me that if they are going to Canadianize by way of private Canadian industry, then they
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
should do it in a straightforward way. Do not tack all over the place. The government should have some tough Canadian ownership rates. If we do not have some tough Canadian ownership rates, we will have what the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Island (Mr. Manly) said a moment ago-that Imperial Oil will be going into the Beaufort Sea involved in a consortium of companies and the paper consortiums will be doing all the work.
During the committee hearings we were told by representatives of Home Oil that Home Oil goes where it can get the best return. Home Oil will go to Australia, the North Sea or wherever. Home Oil is not perhaps as interested in Canadian-izing or exploring in Canada as we may want them to be. Home Oil's representatives said they would look at the north but Home would be part of a consortium of companies. We will have the same old gang going up north. It will include Gulf and Imperial, which is the same old gang.
This amendment points out one of the defects in the government's energy program. It shows one of the patterns that has emerged from the government's energy program and that is the pattern of backing off. When there is pressure from the industry, the government backs off. That is why the federal government gave the industry $2 billion the other day. The government then sells out. It has sold out on consumer prices. Along with the Conservatives, the Liberal Party is a high-priced party in Canada. The Liberals are even worse than the Conservatives because the Liberals are not going to give any money back as an energy tax credit to low and middle-income people. Instead the government is going to give $8.9 billion in grants to the oil companies.
This money will be given mostly to the large companies because the large oil companies are the ones that will go north in phony consortiums. That is why we have brought in this amendment. If the government wants to pursue this form of Canadianization, let the government bring in some tough Canadianization rules. As I have said before, the government should not be backing off and doing things by quarters when the government could be doing it in total.
Canadians are ready for leadership in Canadianization. I do not agree with the Conservatives in this debate when they pooh-pooh Canadianization. Canadians are ready for it. I think Canadians want public ownership. They want us to use Petro-Canada. David Lewis, Tommy Douglas and the rest of us in the New Democratic Party dragged the Liberals kicking and screaming into bringing in Petro-Canada. Now that we have it, why do we not use it? Why give $8.9 billion to companies that say, "We are for free enterprise; we want to get the government off our backs."? Let the government get off their backs and not give them this $8.9 billion. The government can give the money to people in my riding in the east end of Vancouver who had trouble last winter paying their hydro bills. Luckily, we had a mild winter in Vancouver.

We should get the oil companies off the people's backs.

My colleague says we should get the oil companies off the people's backs, but we will not if we give them $8.9 billion. It seems to me it is the other way around.
In any event, this amendment proposes to say to the Liberals "Quit backtracking; get on with the job. Make it tough if you are going to do this, otherwise Canadianization through PIP and COR will simply fall apart." I invite the government to accept the amendment.

Motion No. 6
That Bill C-104, an act respecting petroleum incentives and Canadian ownership and control determination and to amend the Foreign Investment Review Act, be amended by adding immediately after line 38 at page 7 the following:
"12.(1) Notwithstanding this Act, any aboriginal right, title or interest, or any claim under such right, title or interest that any aboriginal people in Canada may have had prior to the coming into force of this Act, in and to the land which is herein described as Canada Lands, continues to exist until an agreement with that aboriginal people is effected which provides otherwise. (2) In this act, "aboriginal people" means those people described in Section 35(2) of the Canada Act."

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. Motion No. 6 is similar to an amendment that was accepted for Bill C-48. It is necessary to assure the aboriginal people of the north that we continue to regard their rights as being paramount. The guarantee in the Constitution is not something they regard as adequate. I think
it is important that we have this amendment accepted. In the native claims policy entitled "In All Fairness", tabled in December, 1981, by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), we find on page 23 the following:
Lands selected by Natives for their continuing use should be traditional land that they currently use and occupy: but persons of non-Native origin who have acquired for various purposes, rights in the land in the area claimed, are equally deserving of consideration. Their rights and interests must be dealt with equitably.
Other basic access rights must be taken into consideration: rights of access such as transportation routes within and through a settlement area; rights of way for necessary government purposes; rights of access to holders of subsurface rights for exploration, development and production of resources, subject to fair compensation as mutually agreed either through negotiation or arbitration.
This places the whole question of Indian land rights and aboriginal rights on a par with the rights of big corporations that have acquired financial interests in the area. I think it is absolutely essential that there be some protection for the aboriginal rights of the people of the north. This is in accord with previous guarantees. I urge the government to accept this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak briefly on this amendment. I will perhaps say something about the other motions afterwards. As we are all agreed to the government motions, perhaps we can proceed with them right away and have the vote before five o'clock.
With respect to what my colleague said, it is important that we put something in this bill to recognize that there are aboriginal rights in this particular area. I am amazed how powerful the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) seems to be in the cabinet. He is nodding and saying how he appreciates that. But the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) have completely lost in their dealings on the north. The little white knight of the Department of the Environment has been slain by the dragon of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The Department of the Environment has really been thrown out of the north and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has won the battle and has developed the north in every respect.
The Minister of the Environment should pay some attention to what the native people up there have been saying. He should pay some attention to the fact that if there is an oil spill in the Beaufort Sea-as there will be, although I hope not-as we speed up exploration, we will have an environmental disaster of a proportion that we have never seen before. It will be worse than the blow-out in the Gulf of Mexico, because we will not be able to stop it.
Plug the holes with cabinet ministers. They are sticky enough.

My colleague says we should try to plug the hole with cabinet ministers. In any event, what we have tried to do is consult with the Dene people. I understand that the
June 10, 1982

native people from Alaska to Greenland have an interest in the development of the north. They had suggested to us that they have a consultative council so they could be consulted at least when the development went ahead and when the minister authorized grants and directed exploration in the north. They felt they were not listened to when we debated Bill C-48. They do not have the kind of lobby which the industry has. They do not have the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), the pimp of the oil industry here, to raise arguments for them. They do not have money to put advertisements in newspapers.
