He said: Mr. Speaker, the most salient point of this debate is freedom of information but there is an underlying point and that is the profligate spending of the Grit government on the other side of the House; in reality, it is the total squandering of taxpayers' dollars and then not wanting to account for it.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Maltais) did not wish to tell me, and thus did not wish to tell the Canadian people, on whom, where and why the International Development Research Centre spends Canadian taxpayers' hard-earned dollars. The IDRC has budgeted for 1982-83 to the tune of $59 million but the government does not want to answer questions about it.
There is no open government on the benches opposite; there is no freedom of information with the government and there is no autonomy either. One thing there is, however, and that is moral turpitude. The government does not believe in or have any appreciation for the British democratic system of responsible government. The Freedom of Information Act, Bill C-43, has finally come before a committee but the warped thinking of the Liberals leads them to want to amend it to make the public establish its right to freedom of information. It looks as if the government wants to make a whole list of cabinet exclusions and exemptions to protect cabinet ministers even further and make them even more irresponsible. Bill C-43 could mean that taxpayers seeking information may be subjected to a judicial review before they can obtain information from this arrogant, unbending and unrepentant government.
This is the government that has destroyed our currency, destroyed our international credibility, that has given us the highest interest rates in history, that will not help the jobless, that will not help the mortgage holder and that will not help the farmer or the small businessman. Now it will not give out information on increased aid spending.
I do not think there is a Canadian alive who does not want to give aid to Third World countries if and when that aid is desperately needed, Mr. Speaker. At the moment, however,
1,250,000	Canadians are unemployed. Interest rates are high. A business is going bankrupt every 20 minutes in this country. But do we cut down on foreign aid, the irresponsible spending
International Development Research Centre
part of it that does not make sense? No, Mr. Speaker; instead we increase it.
Let us examine the reasoning behind my request for the production of papers, Mr. Speaker. First, there is the fact that the Liberal Party has been infiltrated by a cell of left-leaning demagogues headed by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Second, this government is made up of a bevy of profligate spendthrifts throwing taxpayers' money away with abandon, particularly to leftist states. Third, it is a government that was elected to govern, not to rule, but it has been ruling by orders in council and by secrecy for the last 14 years. It is a government which is not responding to the will of the people. It is a government that is not supplying information not only to the people but to the official opposition, of which I am proud to be a member.
The government is bankrupt of new ideas to increase our own productivity. That is what is needed before we can help any Third World countries and before we can help ourselves. If we are to be successful we must increase productivity and our GNP before we can aid the Third World in a constructive manner.
The government, in the guise of helping the Third World, has mismanaged millions of dollars through Cl DA and the IRDC and has flagrantly assisted left-wing regimes with Canadian taxpayers' money. All of this is taking place at a time when we could have used this funding. That $59 million could have been pumped into agri-bonds, into small business development loans, into farm credit, used to help people with their mortgages and to stave off bankruptcies.
Canadians want to know where their tax dollars are spent and so do members on this side of the House. They want to know who is receiving the aid. They want to be assured that it does not go to unstable or communist regimes. We want the government to spell out who receives our largesse and why they receive it. As our businesses go bankrupt, as farmers fail and as interest rates go through the ceiling and our dollar sinks to the lowest depths, we want to know. If the freedom of information bill were before us, this debate would probably not be necessary.
In the time that I have been in this House expenditure abuses have only come to light through the brown envelopes that find their way to members and occasionally through the Auditor General's report. The synopsis provided by the IDRC is vague if not incomprehensible. Cl DA is a horror story and everyone in Canada knows that. The figures show that.
An hon. member opposite set down question No. 3,515 on the Order Paper asking the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) how many people work for the Canadian International Development Agency, how many of them work in Ottawa and how many in countries where the agency gives aid, as well as the total salaries for staff outside Ottawa and in Ottawa. The answers are shocking, Mr. Speaker. In Ottawa-Hull 1,003 bureaucrats work for CIDA. In countries where CIDA provides development assistance, 54 people are employed for a total of 1,057 people. For the fiscal

June 10, 1982
International Development Research Centre
year 1981-82 the salary costs, including overtime and other costs, are estimated at $32,400,000. This is at a time when the government preaches restraint.
I should like to mention a few examples of where our aid money goes, Mr. Speaker. Ethiopia must have the best sorghum crop the world will ever see, because in four separate funding projects we gave that country a total of $1.36 million. In a dozen aid projects to the left-leaning Ethiopia the IDRC invested a total of $3.2 million.
I should like to know why we invested $290,000 to develop the impact of tourism on Asia? Is that very important to Canadians who are losing their jobs? Why did we invest $73,700 in the Cuban lobster fishery? Tanzania, under the dictatorship of Mr. Nyerere, was a favourite target of IDRC. It is one of Canada's favourite aid clients. In the three fiscal years of 1978-79, 1979-80 and 1980-81, Canada gave this Marxist dictatorship $91,541 million. Of this, $78.92 million was in grants-not loans, but grants. If that $78 million had been put into small business or agriculture in this country, we would have started getting back to work again.
We gave that friendly little country of Iran $292,000. We gave Algeria, with its dictator, $380,000. In separate funding and nothing to do with the $100 million we already gave, Mr. Manley of Jamaica received $828,000 for four projects. Mali is another left-leaning country and it received $1.13 million. El Salvador received $385,000. The friendly Belgian Congo received $105,000 for the improvement of nut crops. The biggest crop of nuts is sitting opposite, Mr. Speaker!
All of this money was given to hostile regimes and dictatorships at a time when Canadians are out of work, mortgages are uncontrollable, and interest rates make it impossible for anything to work right-even with all the grease that the government applies.
These are just a few of the giveaways that I wanted to address, which is why I asked for this debate. We would like to know why this money is being spent, where, what the countries are, and we would like to see all the documentation to show that it is nothing but profligate spending. CIDA's budget last year was $1.45 billion, escalating to $1.74 billion this year. This is double the per capita contributions of the United States. What a fallacy! President Reagan has cut foreign aid to $5.1 billion; ours has gone up to $1.74 billion, and the government wants to raise it to 0.7 per cent of the GNP by the end of the decade.
How many more billions will that be to build statues, to build sewage systems which fall into the sea, to help Haiti cancel it because it was not managed property? We are giving the Czechs a $300 million sweetheart loan to build a phosphate pulp mill, the better to compete against our forest products industry. We are helping to modernize Cuba's airports, the better for them to launch bombers and fighters and provide smooth landing for planes from the U.S.S.R. We are lending the U.S.S.R. $1 billion at fire sale interest rates, perhaps as
low as 7.8 per cent, for a gas pipeline. It is a litany of trial and error and mismanagement. These are not just my words, believe me. All you have to do Mr. Speaker, is look at the 1979 Auditor General's report which says:
A significant factor affecting CIDA's Estimates is that it has been obliged to obtain legal authority for its operations through appropriations acts, because there is no act of Parliament establishing the Agency and delineating its authority.
Imagine, they are spending almost $2 billion of taxpayers' money without authority. It goes on:
For example, in the 1979-80 Estimates, Vote L40 will appropriate SI to establish authority for a statutory item to purchase shares in the Inter-American Development Bank.
Another one of those dollar votes where you have to be a Philadelphia lawyer to understand the bookkeeping principles of this government. What does that $1 vote mean? It goes on:
The estimated cost of these shares is $310 million (U.S.).
That is what is hidden in there. The report says:
The present form of the Estimates is prescribed by the Treasury Board. We found several weaknesses in this format that limited CIDA's disclosure of information to Parliament.
That crew across the way goes on and on. Mr. Speaker, let us look at Volume I of the Public Accounts of Canada for the year 1981 and really get into it and see what is going on over there, and why we are in the trouble we are in. It says:
Loans to national governments consist mainly of the loan to the Government of the United Kingdom under the authority of the United Kingdom Financial Agreement Act, and special loan assistance to developing countries.
Table 6.8 presents a summary of the balances and transactions for the various types of loans and advances that were made to national governments including developing countries.
It makes very interesting reading. For instance, the first item is "China-Finance $49,426,118". A little later on it says:
An interest-free loan to China was authorized under the Export Credits Insurance Act.
We borrow money at 17 per cent or 18 per cent and give $750 million to the Governor of the Bank of Canada to prop up our dollar, but we can lend money to China interest free. Then there is Greece, March 31, 1981, $6,525,000. Then it says:
An interest-free loan to Greece was authorized by PC 1932-2630.
We know what they are, those little orders in council. Parliament does not get to hear about them. Then it says:
Partial settlement has been negotiated as at April I, 1981, and parliamentary authority to write off the balance during 1981 -82 is being sought.
It says "partial settlement" and "write off the balance". Write it off, boys! We have all kinds of money. We can go out and borrow more and put some more people out of their homes. Then there is Jamaica, $25 million as of March 31, 1981. This was extended August 9, 1981, with interest at 8.875 per cent.
I can go on and on with this absolutely damning litany, Mr. Speaker. Governments do not make money, governments spend money. When they spend it in this way, they should be turfed out. It is a sin.

We cannot help home owners, small business or the farmer, but would you believe it, we can give 30, 40, even 50 year interest-free loans to other countries. When you look at those countries it makes very interesting reading to see the way they lean, because the ones that get the most attention are the ones that are the farthest to the left. Chile, Cuba, Algeria, Argentina, Belize, and on and on down through this litany of horrors until you come to a total of $2,149,431,850. That is what the government is doing with the hard earned taxpayers' money, borrowing it and giving it away.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, there is no one who does not want to help the Third World. But before anyone can help anyone else they have to be able to help themselves. That means pouring money into Canada for jobs and increased productivity, until we get our GNP up and then we can start to give it to the people, but only those who need it. These countries I have just mentioned certainly are not the people who need it. Take a look at the 1982-83 estimates. The government expenditure plan says:
Canada has traditionally been regarded as a country with a high level of active concern for international development.

The government has announced its intention to increase its level of Official Development Assistance with a view to achieving a target of 0.5 per cent of GNP by the mid-1980s and 0.7 per cent of GNP by the end of the decade.
In the last three months our GNP has gone down 1.8 per cent. Where is the sense? It says further:

If half that were spent on creating jobs, on small business and agri-bonds, on reducing interest rates, what would it do for this country and our unemployed? It is very interesting, Mr. Speaker, to see what CIDA's budget is for 1982-83. It is going to be a nice tidy $1,296 billion, up $188.8 million from 198182. it. Tighten your belts. What a laugh! We will build another statue in Algeria, give a little more money to Belize and the skindiving buddy of the Prime Minister.

That is another beauty. We have a finance minister who is now the patron saint of Belgium for buying Petrofina stock at twice the price it should have been. The questions I put on the Order Paper to have answered are: Who gets that money; what parties do they belong to; what countries do they belong to; and are they communist states? We on this side of the House want to know. The people of Canada want to know. People want their interest rates brought down. People want their mortgage rates brought down. Mr. Speaker, in presenting his ideas about development assistance today, the hon. member opposite has polarized his argument. He calls upon Canadians to choose between assistance to the needy at home and to the needy abroad. There is no need for such a choice. There is nothing mutually exclusive about providing assistance to those in our own society who require help and providing assistance to those in other countries who also need help. The great majority of Canadians support both such activities. We are not a people so devoid of a sense of responsibility for our fellow man that our sense of responsibility, that our sense of compassion, abruptly ends at our own borders. We are working at home to help ourselves but we are also working abroad to help others in need.
The hon. member opposite has directed our attention particularly to the activities of the International Development Research Centre. 1 welcome the occasion to say a word about the remarkable accomplishments of the centre during the decade since its inception. The IDRC unfortunately is not an institution well known to the Canadian people. I say unfortunately because it represents one of the real success stories in the continuing and often difficult, complex saga of international development. Were more Canadians aware of the accomplishments of this unique and imaginative organization, they would share the pride that many of us in the House have in that institution. Many of us have watched with admiration its growth, its evolution and its extraordinary success.
The centre was created some 11 years ago in response to a need articulated by the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson and a major World Bank study group which involved some of most distinguished experts in the field of development assistance. That commission found that of all research undertaken

June 10, 1982
International Development Research Centre
throughout the world, less than 3 per cent was in developing countries. Of even greater concern, some of that research, dictated by traditions of former colonial powers, was centred on activities not of direct interest to the developing countries themselves.
The commission accordingly recommended that urgent steps be taken to enhance the capacity in developing countries for indigenous research. The accuracy of the commission's assessment was amply borne out a decade later when the prime request of the developing countries at the United Nations Conference on Science and Technology on Development in Vienna asked the industrialized countries for assistance in enhancing their own indigenous research capacities. I recall that the Canadian government spokesman at that conference, the Hon. Martial Asselin, pointed out many of the accomplishments of the IDRC. The government of the day pledged additional resources to permit the centre to undertake a new program of linking needs of developing countries with Canadian research capacity. That new program has now been launched with the provision of funds by the present government scheduled to begin this fiscal year. It was, incidentally, at the Vienna conference that the International Development Research Centre was held up as an example for other industrialized countries capable of providing assistance to the developing world.
In short, from the time of its creation in 1971 until the present, IDRC has enjoyed all party support in this House and the continued confidence of Canadian governments. From the outset, the IDRC has been directed by an international board of governors as provided in its statutes and has concentrated its efforts on what has come to be called the "basic needs" sector. The centre consists of four major program divisions, the largest of which is devoted to agriculture and related nutritional sciences. Another of the divisions deals with health sciences. A third deals with social sciences and the fourth deals with information sciences. In all four divisions, concentration is on those persons living in rural areas of developing countries. In the agriculture sector, for example, emphasis is on the production of food crops indigenous to the area and not to cash crops planted for export, as was frequently the policy of colonial governments.
The International Development Research Centre has assisted through its efforts improvements in such crops as cassava, sorghum, millets and a variety of grain and legumes of sometimes exotic but always of a nutritious nature. Additionally, the centre is active in forestry and agroforestry, aquaculture, animal production and in post-production systems, including harvesting, drying, storage and milling of grain. In this respect, the centre was a charter member and continuing contributor to the consultative group on international agricultural research. For a lengthy period, the first president of the centre served as the Canadian member on the technical advisory committee of that group. The current president serves as a member of the board of trustees of the International Food Policy Research Institute.
In the health sciences, the centre's activities deal with such areas as health care delivery services, co-operation with the World Health Organization tropical disease program, and with sanitation and water purity questions. In the social area, the centre has concentrated on funding of research in a broad range of sectors, including science and technology policy, economics, education and associated problems. These studies have assisted developing countries to formulate wise policies leading to the design of more effective development strategies.
The information sciences division, the fourth which I noted, was created to assist developing countries in the accumulation, storage and retrieval of invaluable research information. It has done so in several successful ways, including the design of a bibliographic data management system for a mini computer which has proved to be highly sought after not only by developing countries but, on a licensing basis, by institutions in developed countries.
During its continuing evolution, the centre has kept two objectives in mind. One is to assist developing countries in the solution of their particular problems, but always to do so in a fashion that enhances the indigenous research competence of scientists and technicians in those countries. Accordingly, the research is chosen by experts in the developing countries and almost in its entirety carried out there by them. Hence, the experience gained stays primarily in the developing countries. The problems dealt with are best known to the scientific communities in those countries.
There is every reason to understand, therefore, why so many other countries have emulated the lead of Canada and have created institutions similar to the IDRC. I speak of the United States, of Sweden and of Germany. I am delighted that some Canadian publications have recently begun drawing to the attention of Canadians the accomplishments of this little known but highly effective organization.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words today about the International Development Research Centre and about development in general. Of course, development is a word which is difficult to understand. 1 have difficulty understanding it; practically everyone has a different understanding of the word. I am sure my understanding is somewhat different from that of the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) who introduced the motion which is before the House today.
The hon. member for Simcoe South made quite a scathing attack on the whole program of development which is being sponsored outside Canada. I do not share his ideas. I am sure he realizes that we have quite different views about development in the world.
When a recession begins in a country such as our own, the step below us in the developing world has already reached total depression. If the country is ready to help at a time when it is in good financial circumstances, it is probably helping a group already faced with a recession. The factor we use to indicate recession, 8 per cent to 14 per cent unemployment, is often 30
June 10, 1982

per cent to 60 per cent unemployment in countries which are recipients of development aid.
The word "aid" is also very difficult to come to grips with. I personally believe that the most difficult action for a human being, a group of people or a country, is to aid in a positive manner. How do we aid someone? How do we aid a friend, a wife, a husband or anyone? Almost invariably when someone is in the position of being able to aid, a relationship is established which is at least difficult if not impossible. The question of how and when aid should be given should be studied in great detail, particularly when it comes to international questions.
The present situation is such that there are now four billion people in the world, which perhaps will grow to six billion by the end of the century. How do we feed, clothe, help and house those numbers? How do we help cure the economic problems with which these numbers of people are faced? This is why I believe the IDRC in itself is an instrument, a tool or a possibility to bring about a study to discover how aid can be given.
The International Development Research Centre is located very close to the House of Commons. It is approximately a five minutes' walk from our front door. I suggest to all hon. members of the House, and in particular the hon. member for Simcoe South, that they should visit this centre to see what takes place there.
Back in 1975-76 I had the privilege of receiving a fellowship from the IDRC. Ten such fellowships are given each year to Canadians who are middle-aged and are not working full-time in the area of development. I met those qualifications, and I happen to be one of the ten who received a fellowship in 197576 prior to coming to the House of Commons. I did not even have a thought of entering politics at the time.
Also at that particular stage of my life I had the advantage of studying an area with which I was personally concerned. I am referring to the question of aid, in particular, aid given by volunteer groups in Canada, non-governmental organizations such as church groups, service groups, CUSO and other such organizations. 1 believe this form of aid is closest to the hearts of Canadians. 1 studied how such aid influences the development process in other parts of the world. It involves a very difficult series of steps.
After the period of a year I wrote a book on the subject. I will give a copy of it to my friend, because I attempted to describe the difficulty of the process in it. One of the greatest problems associated with aid is that sometimes there is too much good will and not enough know-how. This is why I turn to the IDRC which has the know-how to learn the process of bringing qualified people from around the world to study particular situations. To my mind this is really necessary and has been very, very well done by the centre.
I have also had the privilege of visiting some of its secondary centres in South America, Colombia, Singapore and Asia where they experiment with the development process to find ways to produce food and to help people to provide for themselves. For example, I saw fish experiments when 1 travelled
International Development Research Centre
with the North-South committee to Singapore. The experiment involved the production of protein from shellfish, not in tonnes per acre but in tonnes per square foot. They were finding revolutionary ways of producing food. For that reason the North-South parliamentary task force recommended to Parliament that the government increase the funding of IDRC in order that it may more fully realize its very considerable potential.
The task force was represented by all three parties of the House. I am glad at the way in which the centre is involved in aid, and I am glad that aid is continuing to grow. The report of the task force indicated that another major problem in Canada was the question of education in the area of international aid. How do we bring about the education of our people to ensure that aid is not thrown away, as my hon. colleague said?
In reality most aid never leaves Canada. Most of the money goes to Cl DA and remains in Canada. In fact, the statutes indicate that 80 per cent of bilateral aid must remain here. It is called tied-in aid. It is money used to buy things in Canada for other countries. The notion that nothing is brought into the economy in this area, as my hon. colleague said, is just not true. 1 do not believe it is so. Most of the money stays right in the country.
In the few moments remaining, I should like to tell a story about my colleague and I when we were at the United Nations a year ago. He suggested that we should go out to dinner together in New York and that I should recommend a restaurant at which to eat. I said, "Let us go to a Brazilian restaurant", and I suggested that we should order feijoado. He, his wife and I enjoyed this dish, at which point I told them that it was comprised of sheep's stomach, sheep's entrails, beans and rice. If I had told them before we started that it was sheep's guts, they probably would not have gone. But the point is that we learned a little about another people, which is important in the entire process of development. We must learn how other people do things so that we can help each other around the world.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak on the third and final reading of Bill C-104. I hope that what 1 have to say on this matter will be heard by the Canadian consumer. This long debate is coming to a close tonight in the House of Commons, but 1 think it is the ordinary consumer of Canada who has suffered and will suffer as a result of these energy bills. They will suffer in the pocket because they will be paying for this legislation. The beneficiaries will be the Government of Canada, the Governments of Saskatchewan and British Columbia, and particularly the Government of Alberta. The oil industry, which always seems to be there to get part of the benefits, will also be beneficiaries.
I used the word at the beginning of the debate that the consumers of Canada were being hosed. They are still being hosed and they will be hosed in the future. Some day in Canada the consumers will get together and rebel against this hosing.
We are told that Bill C-104 is a government bill which is designed to give $8.9 billion in the form of petroleum incentive program grants to oil companies-Canada oil companies we hope. It is only a hope because one can see by looking at the details of the legislation that it contains flaws which will allow Imperial Oil and its friends to benefit indirectly from these grants. The bill will give money to these oil companies to go to
Canada lands in the Arctic and on the offshore of the east and west coast. However, it will mainly be in the Arctic. The companies will go to those Canada lands to explore for oil and gas.
I would begin my criticism of the bill by referring to a recent article in The Globe and Mail dated June 4. It is headed "Tarsiut Wellflow is Disappointing". The article
states:
Not only did oil flow at a much lower rate than expected, but some analysts thought the well is only "marginally" economical.
It goes on to say:
"The results are encouraging, but they still fail to prove that oil can be produced economically from Tarsiut ... Many investors had hopes for this well, partly because of recent comments made by senior executives of Dome Petroleum Ltd. of Calgary, one of the key partners in the exploration program.
Tarsiut is a well up in the Mackenzie. The government has pinned high hopes on the Mackenzie delta and the Beaufort Sea. Its hopes are so high that a large part of the $8.9 billion it is giving to the oil companies in grants will go to this area. Yet not a drop of oil has ever been produced from the area. It seems to me that there have been no real commercial finds in this area so far.
The government is taking a big gamble. It is gambling with the taxpayers' money, it is gambling with the environment and with the lives of the native people who live up there. One wonders why the government is taking that gamble. Would it not make more sense to spend this kind of money on the conventional industry or in the heavy oil of Alberta and Saskatchewan? I suspect that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) wants to go up to the north in order to move around the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. We are back to the old story of the federal government fighting the provincial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Nonsense.

That is the guiding thrust of this program. It is a power thrust which is perfectly in keeping with the style and substance of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
What will happen if oil is found up there, which I hope it is? It is my hope that it will be found in commercial quantities. We need oil in Canada since most of our oil surplus was exported in the 1970s. At one point half of our daily production was exported and that is why we now need to give $8.9 billion, according to the government, to Imperial Oil and its friends to go up to the north to explore for oil.
"The Journal" is a program which comes on after "The National" on CBC. Mr. Jack Gallagher, chairman of Dome Petroleum, was being questioned on "The Journal" on February 9, 1982. His remarks are in the transcripts of that program. He was asked what will happen if oil is found up in the Beaufort Sea. He replied:
Canada has lived and continues to prosper as an exporting nation, and there's nothing very different about oil or gas or wheat or anything else. If we can prove
June 10, 1982

that Canada has a major surplus of oil. then there is no reason why we won't and can't export a part of that.
There is the thinking. More government money to find oil, and if we do find it it will be exported.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: More jobs.

My hon. friend opposite says there are more jobs. Can you imagine how many jobs in Toronto, in your riding, you could create by putting in S8.9 billion? I imagine that you could retrofit every house in Toronto. You would not need the Beaufort Sea resources if you put that kind of money in Toronto. Every small construction firm in Toronto could be put back to work.
However, this is the kind of policy option that the government is taking. It is opting for the big megaprojects and concentrating on the supply side while ignoring the demand. This is not a new idea. It has been said for the last 10 years that there are more jobs in small scale energy, in alternatives and conservation than there are in these big projects. You can create a lot of jobs for $8.9 billion.
Let me explain how the system works. A Canadian company can get an 80-cent grant from the taxpayer on each dollar it spends. If the company is paying some income tax-this is a problem because many of the companies do not pay income tax like you or 1-it has another 13 cents taken off. Therefore, the Canadian public is paying 93 cents on every dollar for this grant. This is the heart of the Liberals' Canadianization program. They propose to encourage small Canadian companies by providing Canadian petroleum incentive grants, PIP grants.
The government has a very complicated and basically unworkable bureaucratic structure to decide what is a Canadian company. It is called COR, Canadian ownership rate. It is very complicated. It will be difficult for it to work, because the oil companies, which are pretty good at this, have literally hundreds of accountants and smart lawyers who will plan to go around these Canadian ownership requirements-
Good corporate citizens that they are.

-just like Shell, Imperial and Gulf have done all over the world, and they will do it here.
I want to quote what the Consumers' Association of Canada said to us. For one brief moment in the committee we actually did hear from a consumers' group instead of hearing from an oil company group. In its brief the Consumers' Association of Canada stated:
Bill C-104 and the philosophy behind it perpetuate the failed energy policies of the past-namely, that future oil security can be bought through higher prices and subsidies for oil companies.
It warns us about the advertisements we will face, and states:
That is why we see full page newspaper advertisements and multi-million dollar television campaigns sponsored by the petroleum industry.
Do hon. members know of the ad where the hockey player skates on a kind of glass with Gulf Oil, or of an ad where
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
someone is out on the rigs on the Beaufort Sea, or of ads with a message like that? This is the message the Canadian Petroleum Association is taking to Parliament today. And it refers to energy security.
More money.

It wants more money, as if $8.9 billion is not enough. It wants more money. The Canadian Petroleum Association is big oil. It is Imperial, which is owned by Exxon, the largest company in the world; it is Gulf in the United States, and it is Shell. That is the kind of people who are directing policies in Canada. They are perfectly right to conduct business in Canada. There are some very good people, such as engineers and so on, who work for those companies, but Canadian energy policy should not be directed by those particular organizations. Beside them, the consumer does not have a chance.
The government is backing off its National Energy Program. Day by day, it is backing off, and I predict that it will back off more. A year ago we said that it would back off and, sure enough, two weeks ago it announced another $2 billion for the oil industry.
1 want to tell Your Honour a little about how the program works. The PIP program in this bill, these grants which will possibly amount to 93 cents on every dollar, will replace the past giveaways, the superdepletion allowances. The only real difference from the past, however, is that the beneficiaries will be privately Canadian-owned companies instead of multinational oil companies.
We are hearing many arguments from the oil companies on how they are risking their money to find oil in Canada. But I say, on behalf of the consumers of Canada, that these companies have been drilling and have struck it rich, but they have not struck it rich in the Beaufort Sea, not at Tarsiut. They have struck it rich in Ottawa; that is where they have struck it rich. They have struck it rich in Alberta as well. The Alberta government is administering the Petroleum Incentive Program for Alberta. That was part of the deal with Ottawa.
The PIP grants are only the latest aspect of the supply and demand roller-coaster, it seems to me, which has typified the historical pattern in Canada. I think we all understand that the goal of the oil companies is to maximize profits. They do it by demanding higher prices and more tax incentives in order to find more oil and gas. When it is found, they tell the National Energy Board that there is a surplus and that it must be exported to keep their cash flow going.
After the export permits are granted, that 300-year surplus suddenly threatens to run out in seven years. There is a crisis. There is a shortage. Then the oil companies say, "We must have energy security for Canada." "Energy security" is interesting wording. It is basically oil company wording. How do we get energy security for Canada? The oil companies say, "You give us higher prices and you give us more money." It is a Catch-22 situation. It would be amusing if it were not costly

June 10, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
to the taxpayers of Canada. It amounts to $8.9 billion. Just think what we could do with that money in the fields of medicare and education.
In my province of British Columbia people are lining up for hospital beds because we apparently do not have enough money for health care. Students are having difficulty as their loans are being cut back. The government is making it more difficult for students to live. However, we can find $8.9 billion for the oil industry.
1 am attacked as being a radical socialist who suddenly, according to my critics, does not understand the industry. Well, I will tell Your Honour that there are a couple of things I do not understand about the industry. One thing I do not understand is when I hear my Conservative friends and the industry say, "We are in favour of private enterprise. Get the government off our backs." Then they want $8.9 billion of the taxpayers money to explore for oil, and they call it their money! We heard a good submission by Home Oil Company, a Canadian company, which was very instructive. It pointed out that Australia does not have a grant system. Why does Canada need this system? It needs this system because it is part of the Liberal Canadianization goal.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) was perhaps radical in the 1960s, but now, in the 1980s, as he is older, he thinks that this is a bureaucratic and unworkable system, as he said in the House. That is the only thing we have agreed upon in these last two months of debate. It is a bureaucratic and unworkable system.
There is one other thing 1 do not understand, and I am sure some of the Liberal members will correct me if I am wrong. Why does it seem we are in such a hurry to go to the frontiers when there is still action and there are still oil plays in Alberta and Saskatchewan? I point that out to the hon. member. As well, are there not small Canadian companies in the Lloydmin-ster-Wainwright area? That is what 1 am told in Calgary. I am told that that would be a good area to work.
In Edmonton the Energy Services Association told us that they will have trouble supplying services way up in the Arctic, because they feel that the big oil companies will go to their big American contractors and therefore the spin-off jobs will not go to Canadians.
Why are we going to the Arctic so quickly? I know that there has been a decline of conventional oil in western Canada, but it seems to me that there is a Saudi Arabia of oil in the heavy oil in Alberta. 1 think we could go there. We are going to the Arctic because the government does not want to deal with provincial powers. It does not want to deal with Alberta or Saskatchewan. It wants to deal with the Northwest Territories or the Yukon because they are colonies.
Today in this House we introduced an amendment to protect the native people. It was not a radical amendment. Our amendment would have ensured consultation with them to get their views and involve them a little bit in this development. Its purpose was not to exploit them. However the government just rejected it out of hand.
The government is intent on falling into a trap, the trap of a rather strange Canadianization. I think the Canadian people
want Canadianization. As a matter of fact the Committee for the Canadianization of the Petroleum Industry came before the Energy Committee and submitted a statement dated January 24, 1982, after a conference in Ottawa, which stated:
These governments should use much of their increased revenues from oil and gas to benefit Canada by increasing public ownership of the industry.
What is the effect of the PIP program and the Liberal Canadianization program? The effect is to increase private ownership. Therefore the Rockefellers are replaced with the Gallaghers of Dome and the Blairs of Nova. It is no wonder that Dome and Nova are so subservient and interested in the federal Liberal Party and so very uncritical of the government's National Energy Program. They are so clearly uncritical of the program. Where does it get us to replace the large American oil companies by the large Canadian oil companies?
Mr. Speaker, do you know what the largest Canadian oil company is? We found this out in committee. The largest oil company in Canada is Imperial Oil. The largest Canadian company is Dome Petroleum, not Petro-Canada. The Committee to Canadianize suggested, and I quote, "That Canada's goal must be increased"-that is, Canadian ownership-"to at least 75 per cent in Canadian ownership of the vital petroleum industry by 1985, with Petro-Canada as the largest oil company in the country."
As most Canadians know, we have an oil industry that is, or at least was, about 75 per cent foreign owned. In the last year or so, $6.5 billion has been spent, and the Canadian ownership rate has increased only by about 6 per cent.
It is a beginning, I admit that, and in many ways the minister has had a certain degree of courage in bringing in a program, albeit a small program, to try to do something about it.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre, the opposition critic, my counterpart in the Conservative Party, also expressed an interest in Canadianizing the industry. He pointed out, contrary to what I sometimes say about him, that he was a member of the Committee for an Independent Canada, in Calgary. So we all want to Canadianize the industry. How would we do it? I am not sure how the Conservative Party would do it. I have trouble understanding them or getting them to state how they would do it. It seems to me that they say it is going to happen naturally.
The government has said: "We are going to do it by PIP grants, we are going to do it by this Canadian ownership rate." It seems to me that there is another way of doing it. This is what the Committee to Canadianize said, and I quote, "We strongly urge the federal government to acquire one of the four major foreign-control led companies as a new Crown corporation or as a component of Petro-Canada." In other words, if you really wanted to Canadianize, if you really wanted to get 50 per cent control of this industry by 1990, or indeed by 1985,

June 10, 1982
you could do it. But it would take some political courage. Instead of giving $8.9 billion in PIP grants, you could introduce a bill in this House of Commons to acquire the majority interest in Imperial Oil, or Gulf, or one of the other companies. There is support for that amongst the Canadian people out there.
The Committee to Canadianize said they did a poll and the poll indicated that Canadians, by and large, favoured such a takeover. They took a Gallup poll on the question of public ownership. It showed that 55 per cent of Canadians were in favour of taking over one of the big four oil companies, while 28 per cent were opposed. As to increasing the Canadian ownership rate more quickly than the government would like, Canadians were away up in the high 60 per cent region in favour of that. So there is support out there. The government could do that. But instead the government will throw $8.9 billion at the industry. That is the problem.
There are other things the government could do to help this industry, and to stop it from being an export-oriented industry. Let us take natural gas, for example. When the minister was in opposition, before he became known as "Old Ironclad," he suggested that there should be iron-clad guarantees, that we should not pre-build the Alaska pipeline before we had financial guarantees that the whole line would be built. The reason for that, as he correctly saw, was that if we built a large export pipeline, he or some other energy minister would be under all kinds of pressure to export natural gas. And that is what is happening right now in Alberta.
There are other things that we could do, Mr. Speaker. We could broaden the gas market, and the minister has tried this and he should continue doing this, by getting people in Ontario and Quebec to convert to natural gas. We could throw some of that $8.9 billion at further conversion, and we could pay the money more quickly to the people and we might get further conversions to natural gas. Then we could use Canadian gas in Ontario and Quebec and in the Maritimes, rather than export it to the United States.
Also, we could get a proper marketing system of gas, a proration in Alberta, so that some of the little companies would get a better shot at the market rather than the big companies.
You could also put some money into the heavy oil sector through smaller projects. I know that in the recent update the minister has agreed to give certain tax advantages in that area. But a lot more could be done in that area. And it would benefit the small producers rather than the larger oil companies. If it works, you could give some money for oil upgrading.
I do not think that Canadians understand why a government would give $8.9 billion in grants to oil companies. Dome Petroleum told us in the committee that they did not pay any taxes; but they are going to get one third of the grants. That is how we thought the grant was $6.5 billion. They would get one third of these grants in the next three years, which was about $600 million. A lot of the money was being used in that bill in a crazy bid to take over other companies. What are we doing
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
in this country? The banks are financing oil companies and other companies to take over companies, when we have so much need of capital in other aspects. In my province the forest industry is in depression. We will have to consider ways of directing bank investments so that money will be invested in housing and manufacturing and some of the areas where it is needed. What does this bill do? It does not do anything like that.
What do other countries do, Mr. Speaker? Australia does not give grants. In Mexico the industry has been nationalized long ago. In Britain the industry is 50 per cent owned by the British National Oil Corporation, which has the first claim, and a 51 per cent share of oil production. They participate in joint ventures, but they retain control over all the projects.
To whom are we giving control here in this bill? We are giving it to Canadian private firms like Dome Petroleum, which appears to be on its last legs. We are going to give $600 million in grants to a company that is having financial difficulties now. I hope it does not collapse but, if it does, the last remnant of the National Energy Program will collapse with it.
I know that those men had some dreams for the Beaufort Sea. Why are we putting all this money into that? It seems incredible to me.
In Norway, StatOil, the government oil company, can take up to a 70 per cent interest in any block of land it does not already hold, and it is an active participant in controlling things. They have learned, in the other countries, not to knuckle in every time the oil industry cries out. We have not learned that yet. We still have these advertisements in the newspapers and we still have the consumers getting hosed. Mr. Speaker, I said it was inconsistent for the companies to argue that they needed $8.9 billion in PIP grants when they also said they wanted the government off their backs. If they do not want corporate welfare, then don't take it.
It is also inconsistent, I might say, of the party on my right, the Conservative Party. On second reading they voted against this bill. Apparently they are still against this bill. Yet, on December 21, 1981, the opposition critic, the "radical Harv" as they call him now, the member for Calgary Centre, wrote to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde):
The parts of the proposed bill dealing with the Canadian ownership rate and the Petroleum Incentive Program are long overdue.
So there is the Conservative Party saying; "Let us get on, let us give the $8.9 billion."
Right on!

Every day in this House of Commons the Conservative Party stands up and asks for more money for the oil companies. They also want to get rid of Petro-Canada. What kind of program is that? If we are to believe the latest polls, there could be a future Conservative government, and perhaps the hon. member for Calgary Centre will be the minister of energy, mines and resources. What would he do? We should read his speeches. He would give Petro-Canada away.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I do not know about the minister's constituency, but the people in my constituency are ordinary people. The people in the east of the Vancouver-Kingsway constituency are having some tough times right now. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), represents a city constituency. The hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) represents rural areas. My colleagues represent farmers and native people in the north, but we all represent consumers. It is the consumer who has to pay, and the price of gasoline has risen. The average cost of heating a home in my riding has increased from approximately $800 to $1,100 in a very short time. The cost of putting gasoline into a car and driving it for a year has risen from $700 to approximately $800. As statistics tell us and as any senior in Vancouver-Kingsway could tell us-and they have told me-the price of energy has risen 30 per cent in the last year, and it will continue to rise.
If the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is really concerned about the consumer, let him not come into this House with $8.9 billion in PIP grants. Let him go to Premier Lougheed and Premier Devine of Saskatchewan and say to them, "Let's give the consumers of Canada a break." Let the minister and his provincial counterparts forgo the scheduled $2.25 a barrel increase in the price of oil on July 1. For a change let them give the consumers of Canada a break.
We in the New Democratic Party oppose this bill. We oppose giving $8.9 billion to one of the richest industries in Canada. Some small companies are having bad times now, but there are measures we could take to help them. We do not need to give $8.9 billion in relation to the Canada lands. Let us develop some of the heavy oil in Alberta and Saskatchewan. In the next scheduled increase let us give consumers a break at the pumps. Let us see if we can do something for the seniors of this country by way of grants or tax credits. Those are the kinds of things we can do but, instead, the government brings this bill forward and proposes to give the oil companies $8.9 billion. It proposes to pay 93 cents of every exploration dollar and to do that without taking a corresponding equity position.
There is an answer. We can be positive. The answer is to put that money into Petro-Canada, the government oil company, and to put money into conservation, alternate energy, insulation and so forth. That would change the mix. That would be a policy the people of Canada would welcome. The people of Canada are looking for leadership. It looked as if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources finally would start to provide leadership through the National Energy Program and get control of our industry-a vital industry-but instead we have a phony, unworkable Canadianization. It is a sham. It is a
bureaucratic scheme. It proposes to give by way of grants what used to be given by way of tax advantages. It repeats all the mistakes of the past.
I quoted Gallagher in relation to exporting oil. I spoke about exporting gas. We are going to make the same mistake. We must be a pretty dumb country to export half our oil.
Dumb government.

It is a dumb government. It would have to be crazy to repeat the same mistakes in relation to natural gas, yet that is what this government is doing. For all those reasons we in the New Democratic Party oppose Bill C-104.

Mr. Speaker, I will not take up too much of the time of the House. 1 just want to correct a few of the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). To correct them all would take a great deal of time indeed.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has never let consistency or facts get in the way of a good argument. For example, near the end of his speech he was talking about giving consumers a break. That is a sentiment with which I am sure everyone in the House would concur, but nowhere in the hon. member's remarks did he acknowledge that when a consumer fills up his tank with gas, two thirds of the cost is taxes. If the hon. member wants to be consistent in his concern for the consumer, he should be suggesting that governments cut back on their taxes because it is government taxes to the extent of two thirds which are penalizing the consumer.
The hon. member suggested in his speech that what we need to do is let Petro-Canada take over another big oil company. Petrofina was not enough. The takeover of Petrofina is being paid for by means of a tax paid by consumers. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway should make up his mind. Does he want to tax consumers more in order to provide Petro-
June 10, 1982

Canada with more toys to play with, or does he want to protect the consumer? Try as he might, he cannot have it both ways.
Consistency or intellectual honesty will not get in the way of the hon. member's arguments. He thinks it is terrible that all those takeovers occurred last year. I agree with him. I think they contributed nothing to the country. They contributed not one job and not one barrel of oil. Canadianization was the hallelujah chorus of the government. That was a marvellous thing, but in the process many very good companies have been decimated, and nothing has been gained for the country in terms of jobs. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway agrees that all those takeovers were terrible.
Private takeovers.

Then he turned around and said Petro-Canada should take over some more companies. He can have it one way or the other, but he cannot on the one hand say takeovers are terrible because they do not create new jobs or find any new oil-they just use up valuable capital-and on the other hand say, "I want Petro-Canada to do that thing which I have just described as a terrible activity." Yet that is the gist of the argument of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. It is unfortunate he did not feel the necessity to be a little more intellectually honest in his arguments. He is a socialist, a social democrat, or whatever name they apply to themselves these days. That is fine. That is a legitimate political point of view. It is a philosophy which has succeeded nowhere in the world in terms of bringing better standards of living to the people who have lived under it.
What about Germany and France?

Both those countries were doing a lot better when they were under Christian Democrat governments or Gaullist governments than they are doing under socialist governments. Under the Christian Democrats, Germany had one of the highest growth rates in the world. Since the socialists took over they have one of the highest unemployment rates in Europe. If the hon. member wants to use Germany as an example, he will find it performed marvellously under the Christian Democrats and not so marvellously under the Social Democrats.
The one country that has had a consistently outstanding economic performance in the last two or three decades is Japan. It has had a conservative government through all that time.
It has had a little economic planning as well.

If the hon. member were being intellectually honest, as opposed to reflecting the left-wing prejudices he learned in university, he would have to acknowledge that economies around the world work better under conservative governments. What bothers me is the distortion of the position of this party as put forward by the hon. member, and the distortion of things that we have said regarding this program. Intellectual dishonesty is not a capital crime in politics or the
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
hon. member would have been decapitated long ago. It is not playing by the rules, however, to distort the position of another person or party deliberately. I have said repeatedly, as the hon. member knows although he refuses to accept my argument, the whole thrust of this program is a disaster.
The National Energy Program dreamed up by those geniuses in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources- who, according to Maclean's magazine, describe themselves as the "enfin" group, that bunch of PhDs that was turned loose to find a way for the government to control the oil and gas industry-proposed the petroleum and gas revenue tax, the natural gas and gas liquids tax, the incremental oil revenue tax, excise tax and sales tax-you name it. It was an increase in taxes in the order of $6 billion per year. To promote Canadianization they proposed giving $2 billion back to the oil industry, biased toward Canadian-owned companies.
That kind of program sounds great if one's only experience is time spent at the University of Toronto under Mel Watkins. If that is your economic training, then it is a great program. But the real world does not work the way Mel Watkins would like it to work and his students are no smarter than he is. They produced a disastrous program.
I see that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has left the House. The truth must be hurting him.
As I indicated in my letter to the minister and to his parliamentary secretary privately, the government has hit the industry severely with these taxes. They affect the junior Canadian companies in particular. As the government's figures show, in the first six months of 1981, Canadian-owned oil and gas companies suffered a 52 per cent drop in income over the previous year. Foreign-owned multinationals suffered a 28 per cent drop in income, so they were hurt. The Canadian companies were devastated by the taxes brought in under the National Energy Program, however. To help ameliorate that somewhat, the government proposed another stupid plan, which will fail, but if that is what it is going to do-then it should at least do it. That was the thrust of my letter, and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway knows that.
All I was saying to the government was, if that is what you were going to do then at least do it. Don't just load on taxes and kill these companies-and a lot of junior Canadian companies were killed, but not the multinationals. They will last longer than the minister or the government or any of us. A lot of junior Canadian companies were killed. PIP grants were one way in which a little bit of activity could be restored to the industry to get the service companies and drilling companies back to work. Perhaps some of the small towns in Alberta which rely on the oil industry and now are dying as a result of the National Energy Program, will have some vigor restored.
That was the reason for suggesting to the minister last December that if this part of the program, to match the taxes he was already collecting, were brought forward we would treat it with dispatch. We certainly would not support it. We certainly would not vote for it, because it is a disaster and it will collapse within two years. I guarantee that. The reason it

A lot of pressure will be brought to bear with simple-minded approaches like his, asking how grants can be given to the industry while hospitals are closing-how $2 billion can be given to the industry when there is a desperate need for a home for unwed fathers or some such thing! That is the kind of statement that will be made, forgetting about the taxes. The pressure will be overwhelming, and the program will collapse.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot resist the temptation to respond to a few of the things the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) had to say about intellectual honesty. I was particularly amused and amazed that he cited the Japanese government as a conservative government which he has reason to admire. One of the reasons that the Japanese have fared so well over the last 30 years is because of the very close relationship between government and industry. This is because of extensive economic planning and the fact that investment decisions have to be cleared by the government. In fact the opposite of what this Conservative Party most often advances is the case in Japan. In his sermon about intellectual honesty I think the hon. member for Calgary Centre would do well to examine his own position, as Socrates said, before he attacks the intellectual honesty of others.
How many Crown corporations do they have in Japan?

Mr. Speaker, of course the monarchy in Japan was disbanded to all intents and purposes some time ago. Whether there are things called Crown corporations or not, it remains true that in Japan there is economic planning of the sort that this Conservative Party has often criticized. That is the reason Japan has the kind of economy it does. And, of course, Japan has b^en having the best of both worlds as far as international trade is concerned. All countries of the western world are concerned about that, but the hon. member for Calgary Centre did not mention it.
We are talking about the National Energy Program today. The NEP is a failure. It is a failure for a number of reasons, the biggest of which is the Liberal Party, which, in its customary way of not wanting to make hard philosophical and political decisions, has tried to go what I suppose they would call themselves-when they are trying to be positive about themselves, which must be difficult these days-the middle
way. And what they have ended up with is the worst of all possible worlds.
The Conservatives and the New Democratic Party have radically divergent but nevertheless internally coherent views of how we are going to develop our energy resources. The Conservative view is that you give the multinationals and others as much money as they say they need in order to find the oil. We say that for too long that particular scheme, which the Liberals have relied upon up until the creation of Petro-Can, saw the public interest being sold out time and again. We want to see these resources developed by the public sector through a PetroCan enlarged by the purchase of Imperial Oil, so we can go about developing our energy resources in a way that is entirely different from what we have been used to until now.
The Liberals, Mr. Speaker, could not make that kind of decision because they have certain economic loyalties to the oil companies and the private sector and because, in the final analysis, they are not that much different from the Conservatives on this issue. The Liberals want to appeal to that growing body of public opinion which says these resources must be regarded as a public utility and not be managed in the interests of the profit-motivated private sector.
In this respect I give the Progressive Conservative Party credit. They know public opinion is against their position on PetroCan and in favour of more public ownership in the energy industry. Yet they persist in this criticism of Crown corporations; they persist in pouring out venom in this House day after day about PetroCan and other Crown corporations. I can only say that if this suicidal passion of that party arises out of a deep-seated principle and objection to Crown corporations, then they have my admiration. I personally believe that is one of the reasons why the government of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) fell so quickly. Their position on PetroCan helped create the political context for their defeat. They could not come out and say, "I guess this is what the Canadian people want". It is not communism, statism, or all the boogeyman things that so many of the Conservative backbenchers want to make it out to be. But no, the Conservatives, being the sort of principled lot that they are, to this very day still get up and pour abuse on what the Canadian people obviously want.
What about the Liberals? I often say the difference between the liberals and the Tories is the difference between smart capitalists and stupid ones. What we have over here are people who want to give the impression that they are doing something about Canadianization, while at the same time making sure their traditional friendships with the multinationals and private Canadian oil companies is kept well lubricated. How do you do that, Mr. Speaker? With lots of money, $8.9 billion worth in this one energy bill alone. So we have this money going out to the private oil companies, and what have we got? We have a national energy policy which does not work.

Instead of public ownership and having our resources developed in an alternative way, we have this huge bureaucracy which-the Conservatives are quite right-does not work? Why? Because the Liberals do not have the guts to go out and set up a truly Canadian energy sector and begin to develop these resources as they should be developed.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Judas sold his soul for 30 pieces of silver. What we see here is a government spending $8.9 billion on the so-called private sector, when it was unwilling to leave in the established programs financing the $2 billion which would have enabled the government to negotiate improved national standards of medicare. For $2 billion this government sold down the river the future of medicare and gave the provinces a club with which to beat the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) every time she opens her mouth about extra billing. But we have $8.9 billion to give to the private oil companies, these great entrepreneurs.
I get a charge out of the Conservative Party; they are always going on and on about entrepreneurship, free enterprise and risk taking, yet the private sector oil companies and others cannot get their nose in the public trough deep enough and fast enough. Then they go out and lecture people about selfreliance, pulling yourself up by the bootstraps, and all this rhetoric. Socialism for the rich and free enterprise for the poor, that is what it amounts to. If you are big enough and strong enough you can get yourself into the public trough with Progressive Conservative approval. But God help you if you are poor, or on welfare, or unemployed, because helping you is demoniacal and evil government spending. When it is government spending to help out the private sector, the oil companies, that is something the government should be doing more of, and indeed the hon. member for Calgary Centre, as far back as December last, was encouraging the minister to get on with the job of providing this money to the oil companies.
I have said, Mr. Speaker, a couple of times now in the energy debate, and 1 am going to say it again because no one seems to have picked it up yet, that the argument we are having about energy in this country is very limited indeed. It is really about who will preside over the last days of the prevailing energy model; will it be the private sector, the public sector, or will it be this bureaucratic nightmare called the Liberal government? Which of those three will preside over the last days of the energy model we have been living in for decades? Sooner or later we must all wake up to the fact that the energy model which now exists will have to be transcended.
We live in a finite world. As long as our energy policy is directed toward the infinite expansion of supply without seriously addressing the demand side of the question then we are living not in a fool's paradise, but a difficult paradise, because you have to spend all this money trying to find that last drop of oil. You have to drill holes irresponsibly all across the Arctic, taking the chance that we may have one of the greatest ecological disasters of all times on our hands. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
earlier today, what can happen up north will make the spills in the Gulf of Mexico and in other places look like kindergarten play compared to what we will have on our hands if we get a blow-out in the Arctic. Yet we are prepared to do that rather than to face up to the fact that we will have to change our way of life. It is as simple as that.
We will have to redirect the kind of money this government is now willing to spend in a desperate attempt to find the last reservoir of non-renewable resources. We will have to begin to redirect substantial sums of money, not token little bits of money for Enertech and that sort of thing, into the development of renewable resources of alternative energy technologies and conservation technologies and of the "will" to conserve. We must have the will to conserve. That is something that will not come easy. We have been taught in this country that we are able to consume, consume, and consume. There will be some difficult transitions because it will not be an easy task. But in that area we are not getting any leadership whatsoever from this government.
People are much more ready than politicians give them credit for to face up to some of these difficult issues. But people want to know that somebody is there who is willing to manage that difficult transition in their interests, not just in the interests of those who happen to own or control our energy resources. We are pouring so much money into the last days of this energy model, and the last days may go on for some time. The resilience of certain mistakes in ways of doing things never ceases to amaze me. Nevertheless, we are at the end of an era. The amount of money which this government, and particularly this minister, who otherwise seems to be an intelligent man, is willing to pour into these last days is astounding. The money that goes into the nuclear industry to keep that Canadian dream alive that somehow we will be the people who will fill the earth with nuclear reactors! To keep that dream alive, we spend millions and millions and millions of dollars to keep our domestic nuclear industry alive and to finance the export of Candu reactors to whomever is willing to pay the price regardless of what they intend to do with the possibilities that having our nuclear reactors on their soil enables them to do.
In this respect I must say, Mr. Speaker, that sometimes those of us who are in favour of Crown corporations realize just how much we need to make Crown corporations more accountable to Parliament, the people and to the political process than they have been under the Liberal government. I am thinking of the nuclear industry in particular. Here we have Atomic Energy of Canada in Manitoba which is doing environmental impact studies on its experimental laboratory for underground disposal of radioactive waste. What has Atomic Energy said? Atomic Energy has said it will not harm the environment. But I did not expect Atomic Energy to say anything else. It is in the business of selling nuclear reactors. That means Atomic Energy is in the business of creating nuclear waste. That means Atomic Energy also has to be in the business of pretending this stuff can be disposed of safely. The same people are involved in all three areas, and some very
