A little while ago somebody across the way said something about jobs. Apart from the consideration that the kind of alternative energy development that we are talking about I think, in the final analysis, will produce more jobs, and more long-term jobs at that, it will produce clearner, less dangerous jobs and it will provide more meaningful work than the kind of boom and bust employment situation which the kind of development the government is talking about creates. In spite of all that, I want to say a word about the whole question of jobs, and development, of jobs and the environment, and jobs period.
We are in a time when a lot of people are unemployed in this country which is an underestimation when over 1 million people are unemployed. Therefore, anything that is critical of job creation has to be very carefully said. But I think one thing needs to be said, and I will say it now. Just because something creates jobs does not make it right. It is as simple as that. There is no moral axiom anywhere that says simply because something creates employment, that makes it right and it makes it wrong for people to attack and criticize a project and say that it should not be happening.
I will use a biblical example to back up my argument. Recall that when St. Paul came to Rome and converted Rome to Christianity, one of the first things that happened was that he put a lot of people out of work. He put a lot of people out of work, those who were making idols. They used to make graven images which had to do with local religion. St. Paul didn't say, "No, We can't Christianize Rome because, by God, it puts people out of work. Jobs come first. Jobs come before morality. Jobs come before the right and jobs come before everything." He said "No, we are going to do this anyway."
I think we have to decide what kind of society we want, what kind of energy development we want and what kind of an economy we want. We have to have the confidence that we will find ways within that framework go give people meaningful work. That is the kind of leadership the Canadian people are seeking. I think my colleagues and I are able to provide that kind of leadership and we are going to be doing that in the weeks and years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just spoke talked about loyalty. I want to say the loyalty of the Progressive Conservative Party is to the people of Canada. Our policies would be fair to the people in every part of Canada with special privileges for none. I think that is the type of policy the people want.
As for the national energy policy, it has been a disaster for Canada. It is a disaster now. I have just a few comments on that and why this bill should not proceed. Action is being moved from parts of Canada into the north land. I have no objection to the development of our north. It is a very worthwhile endeavour. I do object to the fact that it is being done with a view to discriminating against conventional oil in other
parts of Canada. There is no reason at all why some of this money should not have been spent on conventional oil in Alberta, Saskatchewan and perhaps other places. To move it out entirely ignoring conventional oil has destroyed a large number of small Canadian companies. It is not fair and it is not a sound policy. I think the policy should be fair to native people, and it does not appear to be.
A few months ago Bill C-48 placed the ownership of all land in the north in the hands of the Canadian government. Consequently, the opportunity for provincial status for native people in the northwest territories or northland has almost vanished. Once the Canadian government obtains control of the resources and takes off the cream, there is little hope of provincial governments having sufficient finances to operate. It is not being fair to native people.
Also the government is not being fair to native people in connection with land claims. Native people have been in those areas for a long time. They have been through hard times, they have been through difficult times; they have been through some good times and some times of famine. When an opportunity comes for them to have a break, then they should get it. With the work which is going on in the north, I think there should be a definite policy in terms of hiring northern people. This would give them a fair chance at being employed close to their homeland, which I do not think is contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The National Energy Program has taken money out of the pockets of people. If all the taxes which have been enumerated a number of times already could be totalled and were left in their pockets, we would find that consumers would be doing all right. If the money which has come out of the pockets of oil companies had been left there, they would have been able to make it on their own rather than go bankrupt. If the government continues to extract and extract from companies, whether small or big, and to expect them to stand on their own, it will simply defeat the purpose and drive them into bankruptcy. This is exactly what the national energy policy has been doing. They have penalized consumers through taxation on their heating oil. Not only have they penalized those who are working, but those people who are unemployed, crippled, or senior citizens. These people are being penalized because of excessive taxation. Every pocketbook in the country is affected by the National Energy Program, the disastrous budget and high interest rate policies.
I will not make comments about others who believe differently than I do. One's argument is not very good when one starts to ridicule, to call other people stupid, and so on. The country was built by free enterprisers and the vast majority of Canadians today are free enterprisers. I make no apology for being a free enterpriser. Free enterprise, without the shackles of government through excessive taxation, can give the people of the country the highest possible standard of living. In fact, it
June 10, 1982

has given Canadians a high standard of living and can continue to do so, if the government does not continue to shackle it and prevent it from working. Of course that responsibility is on the government.
I hope there will be no ecological disaster in the great north. I do not agree with the current policy, but public money is being spent and I do not want to see a disaster in the north. The government should have realized that the money would have been safe and would have almost immediately brought in returns if it had been used in the area of conventional oil. The situation is entirely different when one looks at the far north. In the area of the Arctic islands tankers are faced with 20 feet of packed ice. No way has yet been found to extract the oil. There might be icebreakers which are big enough, but they have not yet been invented or found. I think they can be found if we are given the time. The industry must find a technical way of raising the oil to the surface, of putting valves in place and keeping them there; of protecting the valves when the ice moves so that the well is not wiped out, of getting the tankers in to load them and of getting them through the northwest passage to market. There are some gigantic problems. I do not begrudge the spending of this money in the north, but some of it should have been spent on conventional oil. It would have kept thousands of people working and scores of companies from going bankrupt both in the oil industry and others.
As I see it the policy has been a disaster for Canada. The effects of the National Energy Program will be felt for a long time before people can start producing and have faith in the government again.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on Bill C-104. First I should like to compliment the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) who worked very hard in committee. Also I should like to refer to exactly what is happening in regard to this energy debate. We are talking about billions of dollars going to the oil companies. We know at election time that the oil companies give equal amounts to the Conservative Party and to the Liberal Party. We know the oil companies have directors sitting on various boards of banks across Canada. Let us not fool anyone as to who is representing whom and who will be given the biggest grants in the programs offered to the oil companies.
1 am pleased and proud of the approach of the New Democratic Party in this matter. On behalf of the almost two million people unemployed across Canada, I should like to indicate to the House that they are finding it very difficult to obtain jobs, to save their homes or the environment around them. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) came into the House and presented a statement which gave an additional $2.5 billion to the oil companies. This was at a time when there were real needs in the lumber industry, in the mining industry and in the automobile industry across Canada. I hope the minister is paying attention to what I am saying this evening. 1 should like to refer to a letter I wrote to him on April 29, 1982, to which I have not received the courtesy of a reply. First, I should like to build up to the reason for writing this letter. On February 10, 1981, Bill C-60 received first
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
reading in the House. On March 6, 1981, it received second reading, was considered in Committee of the Whole and received third reading in the House. Then it went to the Senate where it was amended, and the Senate actually held up the bill with the approval of the minister from April 8 to December 11, when the minister finally had the courage to bring the bill back to the House. On December 11 the House unanimously agreed to the amendments, and then the bill returned to the Senate. On December 18, 1981, Bill C-60 received royal assent. To this day the minister has not given my constituents the privilege of using the provisions of the bill.
Therefore, on April 29 I wrote the following letter to the minister:
During the past year and a half, some constituents in my riding have been trying to negotiate a settlement with the Foothills Pipe Line Ltd. for trespass and damage to their property during the construction of the pipeline in southeastern British Columbia.
I have raised this matter in the House and you are aware of these grievances which the residents wish to pursue through the provisions of Bill C-60.
Bill C-60 received royal assent in December 1981, and I feel it is imperative that your government proclaim this bill so that my constituents can have the opportunity to have their cases heard through its provisions.
If the minister is so concerned about oil companies and ongoing programs, he should take a look at the provisions of Bill C-60 and ensure that the grievances of my constituents, whose property was trespassed and damaged by this company, will be settled. They should be given an opportunity to be heard and to put their case. I urge the minister to proclaim Bill C-60, which amends the National Energy Board Act, so that my constituents will have their day to present their case in a fair manner. I think it is unfortunate that the minister sits on this bill when not only has it been approved by the House but by the Senate. It is now just waiting for the will of the minister to proclaim it and have it gazetted, so they will be given the opportunity to use it.
I also want to say something on behalf of our senior citizens on fixed incomes who have seen their energy bills increase. We have heard some of the proposals presented by the minister with regard to assistance under the conversion program. While he is doing this we are seeing electrical costs in British Columbia going up by as much as 40 per cent. I believe if we are to look at programs that will be of assistance to various groups, we should look at their incomes so that the assistance to be provided can be created by better policies of this government.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have a few moments to make a few remarks about the energy debate and the energy problems which face Canada and the world. For almost the past year, many hours have been spent in the House on the energy debate. There have been many opinions expressed, many ideas and suggestions developed, which I am sure each member delivered with the truth as he saw it.
Since it will only be a matter of minutes until this debate is finished and the whole energy question will be settled for this

June 10, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
session, I would like to go on record as speaking about the future. I do not mean the future six months, six years or even 600 years from now, I am talking about the future of our planet and of the people who will live on it. I feel that as we vote on this energy bill tonight and then proceed with our lives for whatever number of years each of us has left, we must remain concerned about energy. Let us think for a few moments about the people who are to follow us generations from now. What we are doing tonight will affect the lives of all those billions of people to come.
This week I received a petition from a group of people in my riding. The petition began, "We are parents and grandparents-That petition asked that 1 present to the House their concerns about the lives of their children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and 1 have presented that petition. These people did not want their future generations wiped out or destroyed by atomic war. Of course, I am totally in accord with this.
Let us put into perspective this $8.9 billion we are considering handing out to the oil companies in order to preserve, in a sense, the future with respect to energy. I do not believe that $8.9 billion will accomplish that or that all the oil companies in the world can do that unless the people of this planet, including people like myself, all hon. members, every Canadian and the rest of the world, decide that we do only have a limited amount of energy available. Let us not kid ourselves when we talk about new oil and old oil. Relatively speaking, all oil is old. It takes 500 million years for our planet to process and evolve one drop of oil. Oil which is now being formed on our planet will evolve 500 million years in the future. Yet there seems to be almost a madness which, I must confess, 1 share myself about using it all up as quickly as possible. There seems to be a feeling of unconcern about future generations and a feeling that we are entitled to use it all ourselves. I was born into a society which felt that there are no limits. 1 realize now that there are limits.
The oil industry in Canada has evolved during my lifetime. I can remember Leduc and the first pipeline across the prairies. I worked on it. It has not been that long since the industry began to develop. Oil in Canada is a new commodity.
This morning, as I came to the House of Commons, I drove my car. It is a small one.
Japanese?

Not a Japanese car, a small Canadian car. The fuel which went into that car was refined from a process which began almost 500 million years ago. It was burned up and no one will ever use it again. Tomorrow, when many hon. members return to their ridings in an airplane they will see the vapour trail left behind. The fuel which takes us home tomorrow will be finished and never used again. Therefore I must ask myself the moral question of how much energy can I or anyone use if we are to concern ourselves with the plea of those parents and grandparents to look after the future of their children and to leave something for them.
The idea that was common when I was young-although I am not that old yet-that there are no limits to resources is being challenged today. The confidence that there were no limits to resources was prevalent not so long ago. I have seen forests that seem to have no end. However, if one visits the Amazon forest today one realizes it has a limit and an end and is being chopped down very, very fast.
The purpose of my small interjection into this energy debate, which I want to share with my colleagues and anyone else who is interested, is to somehow bring myself to task and to ask others to realize the need to conserve a little bit of what is on this planet for the people who have not yet been born. New sources of energy are just not evolving fast enough. It may not be the most significant interjection in a debate which is to decide how to spend this money, but I would like to see some that $8.9 billion being spent to encourage a company to find more gas to create more traffic jams put to better use. It is said that the world will end in a traffic jam. 1 am inclined to believe that. As you drive on the road today you see one person sitting alone in 2,000 pounds of steel. There are thousands of people who sit in their cars by themselves. Everyone is stopped at a red light with their motor running. It is the beginning of the end.
I would like to end on a slightly different note. 1 had the privilege to represent our party when a Canadian delegation went to Rome for the beatification of Brother Andre and several other people. The leader of our delegation was the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). Although we did not discuss energy, it was an experience which I think we can share. It concerns the city of Rome, one of the great and beautiful cities of the world. I have been to Rome many times in the last 25 years. Rome has changed. There is now a perpetual traffic jam there. People no longer park their cars in single rows. Every street now has a double row of parked cars. You cannot go anywhere in Rome without being in a traffic jam. The beautiful skies of Italy are now smog, and the same situation is true in Rio, Tokyo, New Delhi and Lagos. That is what has happened to the world. While the automobile and the use of its fuel has given us the service which we all appear to want to sustain, we must see what it has done to the planet and our environment at the same time.
Those were a few of my thoughts which I wanted to give the House before we come to the final votes on these bills tonight. Whether we like it or not, these pieces of legislation will influence the lives not only of Canadians today but of their children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren and all our future generations in the centuries to come.

Mr. Speaker, as I understood my hon. friend, we will consider this first stage as a general debate at report stage on the various amendments, with Your Honour's indulgence. I listened with great interest to the previous debate that took place and to the exchanges that flew between the Conservative, and the New Democratic Party members in the House on the previous bill. 1 followed it with great interest when I saw those two extremes on the political spectrum shooting at each other. If we on this side did not intervene much in that debate, it was because, as we say in Latin, in medio stat virtus. We can easily come to the conclusion that the policies pursued by the government stood between those extremes. They were not for absolute, unbridled free enterprise which could exploit people, but, at the same time, we were not out to nationalize the oil and gas industry. We believe that in this country there is room for both a public and a private sector and that the private sector must be kept in a position where it can do what is required in the oil and gas field to ensure that this country will have the security of supply that it needs.
The hon. members of the NDP spent a lot of time referring to $8.9 billion. What they did not mention is that those amounts, spread over a period of five years, are in substitution for tax concessions which existed before. In effect, these figures illustrate a system whereby we will be able to encourage the growth of Canadian enterprises in the oil and gas industry. Moreover, we will not put it all into the Canada lands, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) suggested. As a matter of fact, as he well knows, I spent much time referring to the heavy oil industry in Saskatchewan and all of that, and the PIP grants will go to Saskatchewan and will go to the hon. member's native province of British Columbia. They will not be reserved for the Canada lands.
These are some of the points we could have gone into at great length, but I thought I should at least point out to my hon. friend that he is certainly not adequately representing the reality of the situation by talking as he did, but I am sure that energy is a constant subject of reflection and debate. We will have other opportunities to debate these issues. Obviously I am looking forward to other opportunities to debate with my friends issues with regard to the National Energy Program, the objectives we are trying to achieve, and the assurance that we want to give the Canadian people in regard to fairness of prices and security of supply, and full participation.

Mr. Speaker, we are discussing Bill C-108. This bill has been considered in committee and has been the subject of representations and testimonies by a number of
people, including the Newfoundland Minister of Energy, Hydro-Quebec, the Independent Petroleum Association and several other persons and groups. It has been the subject of debate within the committee and has been amended on a number of points, following representations made before the committee and proposals that were put forward. I believe we now have a bill that is a considerable improvement over the bill we introduced initially, and I wish to thank those who appeared before the committee to express their views, and I also wish to thank committee members for their contribution to the debate on these bills and especially on Bill C-108.
I may recall that one of the basic objections raised, and I am thinking especially of the president of Hydro-Quebec, concerned a provision that would have allowed the National Energy Board to modify existing export licences if public convenience and necessity so requires. The case against this provision was examined very carefully, and we reached the conclusion that the point raised by Hydro-Quebec was a valid one, and that in view of this very serious objection we should amend the bill accordingly. I feel that the subsequent amendment, which removes the electric power matter completely from the purview of the National Energy Board, will settle this particular contentious point.
A more emotionally and politically charged question was also raised, namely, the provisions in the bill that allow the National Energy Board to authorize construction of power lines for interprovincial transmission and which provide new authority with respect to international transmission lines. I referred to the debate as being emotionally and politically charged, because without wishing to give these adjectives a negative connotation-they are a fact of life-I am especially reminded of the testimony given by the president of Hydro-Quebec who appeared before the committee and was asked by my colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway what he thought about this feud between the Government of Quebec and the Government of Newfoundland. Very wisely, President Bour-beau said in his testimony on May 26, 1982, before the committee, as reported on page 2715 of the proceedings, that as far as the so-called power corridor was concerned, he could not care less, implying that it was not a real problem, and that for all practical purposes, it was not a matter of any concern at all to Hydro-Quebec.
Understandably, there have been some wild and wonderful things said on the subject. In Quebec, the Parti Quebecois presented a motion in the National Assembly. There was a long debate and an attempt to raise public sentiment by telling everyone who would listen that Quebec's territory was being violated and that Quebec's autonomy and the inviolability of its borders were in danger. Fortunately, I think the vast majority of the people kept a clear head throughout this debate, and realized that the whole discussion really could not be taken seriously, when the Parti Quebecois claimed that attempts were being made to violate Quebec's borders, to take
June 10, 1982

over its territory or to extend Newfoundland's territory across Quebec, and so forth. Those were, if I recall correctly, some of the expressions being used. As I said in my speech when we first considered this bill, there is no legal difference between the construction of an oil or gas pipeline like the ones being built right now across Quebec and the construction of an electric power transmission line.
These are two techniques for transmitting energy, and following representations which included those by Calgary Power in Alberta and by the Newfoundland government, we had to deal with what the Premier of Newfoundland qualified as flagrant injustice, namely, that we did not put the transmission of electric power on the same level as gas and oil pipelines. In fact, in conferring powers on the National Energy Board, we did not go as far as we did with respect to the transmission of gas and oil. That being said, we still wanted to take into account the actual situation, since we had to deal fairly with the citizens of Newfoundland and Alberta who made representations on the subject, but at the same time, as I said before, the Government of Canada is generally in favour of a negotiated solution and feels that the only valid solution to the differences separating the government of Newfoundland and the government of Quebec is a negotiated agreement between the two governments, and that any other solution, though theoretically possible, would be an absolute last resort, and only if all other avenues had failed would the Government of Canada, the National Energy Board in this case, be called on to intervene, and that all things considered, if the provincial governments were able to reach some kind of agreement, the government would certainly prefer this arrangement to any other kind.
In recent months, I had a number of meetings with my Quebec colleague, Mr. Duhaime, and with my Newfoundland counterpart, Mr. Marshall. I had an opportunity to explore this question with them in detail and I tried to persuade them to come back to the negotiating table and try to reach an agreement. In fact, my colleague, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), urged me to do so, and pointed out that we had to persuade both provincial governments to settle their differences. I understand the hon. member perfectly, because having seen the attitude taken by his own colleagues from Newfoundland, who refused to vote either for or against this bill when the Progressive Conservative Party voted against it on second reading, it is clear that there are considerable regional differences of opinion in Canada on this subject. As the Government of Canada, we felt that we had to recognize our responsibility in this area, and that we did not have the right to hide behind the curtains or remain seated when there is a real and serious problem that is causing Quebecers and Newfoundlanders to lose hundreds of millions of dollars every year and also thousands of jobs which would otherwise be created by construction projects for dams on the Churchill River or on the North Shore rivers.

Once again, Mr. Duhaime asked me to postpone if possible the coming into force of this bill so that he and his Newfoundland counterpart could sit down and negotiate. Obviously, if the two provincial governments cannot come to an agreement after a new effort and a further attempt at negotiation, we shall not indefinitely let billions of dollars' worth of hydroelectric power which is greatly needed by the people of Newfoundland and Quebec flow into the ocean, we shall not indefinitely allow people to remain unemployed when they could be put to work building dams on rivers, we shall not indefinitely deprive the Canadian economy of the very substantial economic benefits this could entail.
I therefore wrote today to my two counterparts, Mr. Duhaime in Quebec, and Mr. Marshall in Newfoundland,

We believe that, with good will from both sides, the two provincial governments could find a beneficial solution. speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again, our position is clear. We are willing to take our responsibilities as the Canadian government, but, on the other hand, we want to make every effort so that the two provincial governments involved will use the time available to them to settle this question themselves. I can assure the House that if those provinces come to an agreement, we shall be the first to applaud and to rejoice since, unfortunately, this issue is now causing great divisions between two provinces which both have a very high rate of unemployment and a great many financial problems generally and which could reap great benefits from an economic development such as that which could result from such an agreement.

I would like to say that in proposing this particular amendment today the Government of Canada will ensure that the provisions of Bill C-108 concerning electrical transmission will not come into effect until six months after the passage and the proclamation of the bill. This is being done in order to give one more chance to negotiations during those six months. We favour a negotiated settlement between the two provincial governments. We believe that for technical as well as economic reasons a negotiated settlement for the integrated movement of power from Labrador through the Hydro-Quebec system is infinitely superior to any system of dedicated line transmission of power through Quebec.
From the discussions I have had with the Quebec minister in the last few weeks, 1 have had a very strong perception that Quebec is ready and willing to show flexibility and good faith in those negotiations. I have had an indication from the Quebec minister that as part of negotiations on the development of the lower Churchill River as well as the Quebec northshore rivers the Quebec government would be willing to improve appreciably the payments related to the upper Churchill power. In addition, the Quebec government would be willing to discuss arrangements under which Hydro-Quebec would not be the exclusive buyer of additional electricity produced in Labrador.
1 think these proposals from the Quebec government indicate that that government is genuinely interested in proceeding with dispatch to serious negotiations of the issues dividing the two provinces concerning the production and distribution of electrical power.
As I have indicated, we also believe that the only truly satisfactory way of resolving this dispute between the two provinces is through negotiations covering a broad range of issues dealing with the production and transmission of electricity. We are therefore giving some time-not an infinite amount of time, obviously-to the two governments to resolve the issues which are dividing them at the present time.
1 regret that the opposition parties have opposed this bill at second reading. I hope upon reflection-and in view of this particular amendment-they will revise their position and agree to support this bill which, I hope, we will be in a position to pass tonight, including the provisions concerning electrical power transmission. As I have indicated, in order to encourage both provincial governments to return in good faith to the bargaining table, the Government of Canada is asking Parliament to amend Bill C-108 so that any part of the legislation concerning lives for the transmission of electricity would come into effect six months after proclamation.
The spokesman for the Conservative Party in the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation stated quite clearly and categorically that his party would support such an amendment, and I hope that the New Democratic Party will see fit to do so as well.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, while we are encouraging both governments to return to the table and resolve their disputes, we have also indicated that if the two provincial governments feel that the Government of Canada can play any useful role in resolving the issue, we will be available to them.
These are the main points I wanted to draw to the attention of the House. I urge the House to give favourable consideration to these amendments and to support them and pass this bill with dispatch.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the minister a double-barrelled question. It would seem that Clause 10 might generate conflicts with respect to the new provisions, having in mind the provincial legislation applying to the agricultural sector, that is the environment legislation. Besides, in light of the remarks, the know-how and the evidence submitted by the president of Hydro-Quebec concerning the technical aspects, it must be recalled that in his brief he did state that Clause 10 might conflict with the provincial statutes. Finally, Hydro-Quebec is concerned over the fact that Clause 10 authorizes the National Energy Board to set environmental standards which differ from those of the provinces with respect to international power lines. The construction of those lines is already fully covered by provincial laws and regulations on environmental protection. According to Hydro-Quebec, Clause 10 will open the door to the establishment of different and conflicting systems and the utility company is afraid that certain line sections may be needlessly subjected to requirements which are totally alien to the entire network. That is why, considering that very relevant remark, the people in charge have shown their competence and deserve our full respect. This amendment applies to all provinces, of course, not only to Quebec, let us not think for a moment that it is aimed solely at Quebec. I hope that my colleagues opposite will show no hesitation in supporting this amendment which would greatly improve this measure.
I listened to the minister who tried once more to reassure people by stating there was absolutely no danger of conflict with provincial laws, and I must refer again to his statement on second reading. The minister said that if we looked at the current pipeline experience in Quebec, for instance, we could see that the Trans-Quebec and Maritimes pipeline is now under construction and should reach Three-Rivers before the end of the year, and hopefully Quebec in the next year, and therefore, that the Trans-Quebec and Maritimes company who were building the pipeline under the National Energy Board licence were now expropriating to build that pipeline, and also that the Trans-Quebec and Maritimes company was operating in accordance with provincial legislation now applicable in Quebec, whether it be legislation on environment or protection of farm lands, and so forth. The case of the Trans-Quebec and Maritimes company over these last few months, over last year was used as an example. That company had to comply with applicable provincial acts regulating some forms of activity within the Province of Quebec. The same thing happened when a pipeline was built, whether in Quebec or elsewhere. When lines were extended, the corporation involved complied not only with federal laws but also with provincial laws that might be applicable. What was involved here, and I am still referring to the minister's comments, was that there was a proposal for granting in respect of transmission lines the same authority that now lies with the National Energy Board for pipelines. This meant that the practice followed in Quebec as I said for the gas pipeline by Trans-Canada and Maritimes was the same as in the case of an international interprovincial transmission line, and I shall come back to this.
I remind hon. members that the minister in respect of transmission lines referred to the same power that now exist. There was no problem when the minister spoke on second reading, and once again when he spoke last night before the proposal was accepted. He is now referring to existing authority. Mr. Speaker, under the existing authority the National Energy Board must comply with provincial laws. The legislation would enable the National Energy Board to ignore them, as proposed under Clause 10, which would become Section 11 of the amended act. Therefore, the minister is not quite honest when he states that the authority granted the National Energy Board in respect of hydroelectric power transmission is identical to the existing one.
The minister knows full well that the National Energy Board will have powers that will extend beyond those existing now and the House of Commons will not be in a position to
discuss whatever regulations the National Energy Board will establish. For that reason, and this is a point I feel members will understand, Section 11 of the amended act would enable the National Energy Board to regulate and make its own regulations on environment and farm zoning. Therefore, I will not be made a party to that kind of argument. As stated by Hydro-Quebec in their submission, this might lead to conflicts and will give the National Energy Board the power to establish new environment and farm zoning criteria. Therefore, if the government have any respect for the provinces they will have no hesitation in accepting an amendment to that clause to ensure that the governor in council complies with existing laws, whether in Quebec or elsewhere. This means that any project that might be implemented would need the agreement of the province where it is undertaken. Such an amendment is extremely important for any province and since the project involved concerns Newfoundland and Quebec, I believe that the six dozens of Quebec members will understand the importance of this amendment and will not hesitate to stengthen the powers of this House, because it has become increasingly clear that every piece of energy legislation which has been discussed here would give additional powers to the National Energy Board and therefore reduce the powers of the legislators. I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that the members from Quebec especially will understand the situation in this case, and I am also aware of the interest shown by my Newfoundland colleagues in this issue. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) recalled earlier that some of my colleagues from Newfoundland were not here to vote on the amendment which I had moved. I shall certainly not criticize the position taken by my Newfoundland colleagues about this project, but I would invite the members from Quebec to have as much courage and integrity concerning the interests of their own province as my colleagues from Newfoundland, and if they do, I am not worried about the results concerning this bill, Mr. Speaker.
I do not want to delay the proceedings on this bill. Once again, I have had the great pleasure to hear the minister move an amendment which could allow the governments of Newfoundland and Quebec to come to an agreement. The minister has repeated many times that the best solution would be a negotiated settlement between the two provinces. For our part, we, of course, ask the governments of Quebec and Newfoundland to come to an agreement as quickly as possible and to tax this great wealth for the benefit of the people of the two provinces. There can be no doubt that we agree in principle. Of course, we blame the government for forcing the provinces to do something which normally should be left to the provinces themselves. We have too much respect for provincial priorities and the provinces themselves to give them instructions and set deadlines for them. In the absence of a negotiated settlement, we now have an amendment which could allow the two governments to negotiate diligently, and I believe that both governments have expressed the wish to do so.

The bill dropped the provision in the draft bill and the National Energy Program which promised that a degree of Canadian ownership of energy companies wishing to export oil and gas would be a factor in whether or not an export licence was issued. In other words, they were to consider whether a company had Canadian ownership before it exported gas. It seems to me that this is backtracking from the National Energy Program. It is not in the bill, and I have made the appropriate amendment to include it.
My other amendment concerns the fact that the bill still allows export licences for oil and gas to run for 25 years. In view of the dismal record of the National Energy Board supply projections, we think the maximum is too high. We think ten years would be more appropriate. We still have oil contracts which we are honouring when there is a shortage of oil. I may be wrong but I think there are still some. When we have these long-term contracts and we suddenly discover that the National Energy Board made a mistake in the amount of natural gas which we have, for example, we may not want such long contracts. Therefore I made an amendment on behalf of the New Democratic Party that we reduce the length of the contracts.

Re: Bill C-108, an act to amend the National Energy Board Act (No. 3).

They could have come and discuss with the Quebec representatives and not with the member for Joliette. They could have come and meet the 74 Quebec members. Mr. Speaker, as far as the matter is concerned, certain things must be said. The PQ members have made a big fuss over the corridor issue and for the most part it will be settled through the minister's amendment which gives them six months to negotiate, but those were not the real Quebec claims. Those claims, Mr. Speaker, among others dealt especially with clause 25 which will probably jeopardize their exports and contracts abroad. In connection with the corridor, I would like to quote Mr. Bour-beau:

"I think that you mean corridor that could be built according to this law." I will say it in French.

Cela ne me fait ni chaud ni froid.
Is that clear? Such is the position taken by the president of Hydro-Quebec, as opposed to that taken by the PQ MNAs. It is not the position taken by the hon. member for Joliette, obviously. But since when does anybody think the hon. member for Joliette will do differently than the Parti Quebecois? Under the headline, "The Churchill Falls issue does not worry Duhaime, the newspaper La Presse published an item on May 31 in which Mr. Duhaime is reported as saying that whichever way the case goes, Quebec has nothing to worry about even if the Supreme Court of Canada rules in favour Newfoundland.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the minister and the president of Hydro-Quebec say so. Of course, there are three or four PQ MNAs who want a little publicity, who want to make a show, as I said to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. But our purpose was to meet the needs of Hydro-Quebec and Quebecers, and this is why the Quebec caucus proposed changes, with the co-operation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). A second amendment has been moved this evening, and this will fully satisfy Quebecers. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to satisfy the PQ MNAs, it is a lost cause. Neither am I trying to satisfy the hon. member for Joliette, he is a lost cause. Our concern is with Quebecers, and if the PQ members really were sincere when they came here Tuesday night, they would have approached Liberal members, they would have approached one of us, we were two: the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre) and myself were sitting on the Committee on Energy Legislation. But they never met us. They told us: Delay
June 10, 1982

the bill for us, delay the development of Canada because we, PQ MNAs are extremely concerned with the quality of life in Canada. Of course, Mr. Speaker, everyone knows this is a farce.
Mr. Speaker, as far as the corridor as such is concerned, the minister referred earlier to conditions, the impact on TransAlta, the fact that we are simply trying to have uniform responsibilities in respect of both pipelines and the hydro corridor, on the environmental aspect, Mr. Speaker, at the Canadian government level. I listened to the Progressive Conservative member who referred to his amendment on environment. I am looking at the Minister of Environment (Mr. Roberts). Again, the federal government has absolutely no lesson to take from the Quebec government on environmental protection matters, whether Parks Canada, federal institutions under the Minister of Transport, or others. We have always respected environmental needs, and not only those of Quebec. We have much more severe restrictions because, for all practical purposes, we have no lesson to take from them.
Why an amendment to Section 25? I referred earlier to the representations made by the Quebec caucus. I also referred to the information we obtained, for instance from PASNY and the New York Hydro Power Pool, which were concerned that the export license might be withdrawn. However, further to the representations made by Mr. Bourbeau in committee, and I quote Clause 25 of Bill C-108, "Section 83 of the said Act is repealed", etc. he went on to state, we feel the phrase "public convenience and necessity" has a meaning that is difficult to measure or define, it can be interpreted in all sorts of ways. Clause 25 will complicate our export negotiations, especially excess power sales negotiations, in a situation where this is more and more a buyers' market. Mr. Speaker, the amendment put forward in committee on that aspect simply solves the problem and, for all practical purposes export licences are no more covered by the amendment. For all practical purposes, that was our objective.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider a little more closely the over-all question of the Quebec-Newfoundland negotiations on the development of the Lower Churchill, we find that once again the Quebec government, which for six years now has proved it is totally incapable of negotiating in good faith with anyone, has met with failure. It has proved its weakness during the constitutional negotiations. It has set aside the interests of Quebec and dwelt only on those of the Parti Quebecois. It has failed in its negotiations with its civil service, and we see what such a failure is forcing them to do now, Mr. Speaker. It has failed in all its endeavours, whether interprovincial or international, over that six-year period. Once again, I feel that neither the Liberal nor the Union Nationale governments which preceded them in power have any lesson to learn from that rump of a government. Mr. Speaker, we have seen it fail in its relations with the anglophones of the province of Quebec,
National Energy Board Act (No. 3)
where once again in bad faith, instead of striving towards solutions to please the people, to achieve compromise, it acted in an arrogant fashion. We see this arrogance in the way they negotiate with the municipalities, the Quebec Urban Community, the Montreal Urban Community. Mr. Speaker, it is obvious they do not know how to negotiate in good faith.
What is important with regard to the Newfoundland issue taken as a whole, as the minister pointed out a while ago, is the fact that Quebec and Newfoundland workers want jobs and if no agreement is reached, those jobs will be lost. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, Quebec cannot afford to lose them. It is also true, with all due respect to my colleagues from Newfoundland, that their government has nothing to teach us as far as its negotiating talents are concerned. I think the Quebec government was every bit as flexible as the one in Newfoundland; unfortunately, the two governments have never been able to agree, not only with us, but amongst themselves and with their own employees.
Mr. Speaker, I trust that with the six-month extension the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has granted them, they will now manage to come to an agreement, because the major concern here is not the interests of the Parti Quebecois, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and the hon. member for Joliette would have us believe nor the three or four members who came to Ottawa on a bit of a pilgrimage to visit with them, but rather the interests of Quebecers in this area, Mr. Speaker, as in all other areas, and the fact that those interests are best served by negotiating an agreement in good faith, and not by means of petty demagoguery.

speechtext:
I hope the hon. minister listens to what I have to say. First of all, I would like to point out that it was in second reading that the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) brought in an amendment for a six months' delay respecting the interprovincial power lines. That is on the record. No one can deny that. The next point I will be proving to the minister is that he had to make this change, this delay, and that he may have to make some more changes arising from what I am going to bring forward, because he must get provincial agreement.
Our amendment, which refers to subsection 39(2) of the NEB, would be amended by clause 11, which was clause 10 in the first reading, giving powers over the environmental and safety concerns, public and construction workers, for oil and gas lines. Section 41 extends this to international power lines and, by clause 19.1, would include the interprovincial power lines.

June 10, 1982
National Energy Board Act (No. 3)
Hydro Quebec expected conflict between provincial standards and those standards to be set by the National Energy Board. Under this act, the provinces have extreme concern over the National Energy Board standards versus their own standards. Our amendment would have required the National Energy Board, when formulating regulations under subsection 39(2), to take into account any relevant provincial regulations or law. That is what we are discussing.
This amendment must be considered in the light of the means by which the NEB will exercise its new-found authority. Its main concern is environmental. The electrical fields omitted from power lines and how they affect car radios when cars travel under them should be considered, as an example. The National Energy Board has long been exercising a passive role in this area. International power lines have always been assessed by the National Energy Board experts to see if they meet prevailing standards. The problem is that the National Energy Board did not foresee the need to hire any new people for its new, over-all responsibility in the area of construction safety where our concern is being raised.
The National Energy Board has given no thought as to how it will implement and enforce its standards. It is hiring no additional people. It has taken all these new power lines and the responsibility for them. It does not see the requirement to hire any more people at this time. Even today, it does not employ any construction safety people. The provinces have had that jurisdiction until now. They will be able to apply existing standards, safety equipment and construction procedures, but they do not have the facilities to enforce these standards.
Once this bill has passed into law, the provincial authorities will have absolutely no jurisdiction. They will have no jurisdiction over the construction site of international and interprovincial power lines. At that point there will be an enforcement vacuum. This is something that we raised in committee. We tried to bring it to their attention, but we did not get down to the final point because the government kept ducking around it.
What is happening in this bill is exactly what happened in 1976 when the government put through the Atomic Energy Control Act. The federal government's responsibility was for the health of Atomic Energy workers, but no one considered the uranium miners. The minister will be aware of that. Those people were floating through the gaps in the floorboards. No one looked after them until, finally, the Atomic Energy Commission set the standards and reached an agreement with the provincial governments which enforced those standards. The National Energy Board has admitted that it did not take this into consideration when drafting the bill. It is a mistake and must be changed.
That brings me back to the first point I was making, that it needs those six months to clean up the mistakes and to sit down with the provincial governments and come to some understanding. This bill is another example of the federal government taking more and more power and intruding, more and more, into provincial rights. In this case, Mr. Speaker, they have left the construction workers at bay with no protection from anybody. They have made a serious mistake in this
bill and they must do something about it. The National Energy Board should already have the know-how today before this bill is passed, if they are going to enforce on-site standards. They do not have anyone employed to protect the safety of the workers; they have given no thought to the workers.
This is pretty common with all Liberal legislation. They do not care about the Canadian workers. This National Energy Program has put many of them out of work. Now they are bringing in legislation that will not protect the workers, and the National Energy Board does not have one person available today to look after that problem. The federal government has avoided this because it did not want confrontation with the provinces. Well, Mr. Speaker, they are going to have their fair share of confrontation with the provinces. They have made the mistake and they have left the employees of the provincial Crown corporations unprotected.
They could have had their agreement a long time ago, if this minister had had any belief in co-operation. They could have had the agreement with all the provinces, but the minister is bullying this bill through. It may be that it is his swan song, Mr. Speaker, but when he leaves I hope he remembers that all the electrical construction workers are totally unprotected by this bill. I will be supporting this, and I plead with the other side to support our amendment. I think it is very important. I believe that we must respect the provincial authorities, we must respect their rights, and I urge the hon. members opposite when we vote on this amendment to vote with us.

The amendment in Motion No. 1 that we have proposed at this stage of the game is asking, in a sense, that the law reflect the reality, because the reality is that federal-provincial agreement is necessary to accomplish anything. In the last analysis, it really does not matter who has the upper hand in a legal constitutional sense, because both levels of government have within their capability the legal authority, the constitutional authority, to frustrate the other level of government, if that becomes the course of action that is decided on. Therefore, what we suggest by this motion is that when the federal government makes orders in council in regard to the provisions of this act, they be subject to provincial laws and regulations.
It is really asking that the law reflect the reality of Canada.
I think that having the law reflect that reality and having this House express that opinion will contribute to better harmony between the two levels of government, better responsiveness by
June 10, 1982

the government to the needs of Canadians and better government for Canadians.
The minister proposed a couple of amendments, one of which is fairly technical. One relates to a six months' hoist. That one is exactly the same as the amendment our party proposed on second reading, which the Liberals voted against.
1 am pleased to see that they can learn, albeit slowly, and have come around to recognize the wisdom of putting in at this point in time that period of six months during which it is hoped that sincere negotiations can occur between the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland and that that question of the Labrador power can be resolved in the way things must be resolved in this country-by way of agreement and not by the use of legal muscle, or electoral muscle, or otherwise.
The great preponderance of concern about this bill has dealt with the question of electrical power transmission, the export of electrical power and so on. That has been the issue which has dominated the public and private debate. There has been the expression in the House and elsewhere that the issue was one of the province of Newfoundland wanting a corridor across Quebec so that they could export Labrador power, and the province of Quebec resisting that. That really is not the truth, Mr. Speaker. The reality is otherwise. I have in my hand a copy of a telegram from British Columbia Hydro, which says that the British Columbia Hydro Power Authority is greatly concerned and objects to the provisions of this bill.
We had before the committee, tabled with the committee, a letter from the government of New Brunswick, indicating that the government of New Brunswick is concerned and opposed to this bill. We had representations-

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Not from the government of Nova Scotia.

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT (NO. 3) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
-from Hydro Quebec expressing their concern. So we have a situation where we have the government of Quebec, yes; the government of British Columbia, yes; the government of New Brunswick, yes; all opposed to this bill. So it is simple minded, and I do not think it contributes to better understanding, to say that somehow this bill has to do on the electrical side exclusively with this Quebec-Newfoundland problem, and that the government is trying to respond to one of the legitimate concerns of the Province of Newfoundland in its attempts to develop its hydro-electric potential.
In all of this debate about the electrical power aspects of this bill people have missed the fact that this bill also affects the oil and gas industry very substantially. There are some provisions in this bill which, in my view, are undesirable, if not offensive.
Clause No. 17 in the bill as reported by the committee indicates that decisions of the National Energy Board under Sections 52, 53 and 54 to change the tolls or pipeline tariffs can no longer be appealed to the federal court. Up to now, when the National Energy Board made decisions respecting the tolls that a pipeline may charge for transportation of its gas or oil, there was the ability to appeal the decisions to the federal court as part of national judicial system of the country. This bill would amend that and remove that right of appeal. Why, Mr. Speaker? We never received any adequate reason
National Energy Board Act (No. 3)
for that. Of course, if you are big brother, it is nice to know that your decisions are final and that no one can appeal your decisions to another body and have them overturned.
Clause No. 18 would allow the National Energy Board to order a pipeline or gas distributor to transport someone's gas on a common-carrier basis. That could be a desirable thing, but it could be abused, Mr. Speaker. There are situations where, because of the way the legislation is drawn, a municipal distribution company, for example, could find itself in the position of being ordered to transport someone's gas, to its own detriment. One can envision a large industrial consumer pruchasing its gas supplies directly from a gas producing company and having the National Energy Board order a distributor to distribute it. That could be very detrimental to the distribution company, other consumers and so forth. There should be some better definition of that part of those changes. It is not there.
Clause 26 of this bill contains provisions which can only be described as exceedingly offensive. The original bill given first reading in this House on April 7 of this year stated in Clause 25 that it would amend Section 84 of the old National Energy Board Act. Clause 25 says:
Subject to subsection (2) and the regulations, the Board may by order, with the approval of the Governor in Council, revoke or suspend a licence if
(a)	any term or condition thereof has not been complied with or has been contravened; or
(b)	in the opinion of the Board, the public convenience and necessity so requires.
This bill says that the governor in council can in fact cancel an export permit when the public convenience makes it necessary. What is the public convenience?

That is right, nobody does. The public convenience will be defined by the minister and his minions. It can mean whatever they want it to mean. Understandably, there was a great deal of concern expressed about that provision that a contract could be cancelled. A company could get a contract to export some electricity or some natural gas and invest, these days, billions of dollars on the facilities to transport those energy commodities and then find that that export contract could be cancelled when the public convenience dictates. How can a company justify that kind of expenditure when a contract can be cancelled on the basis of what the minister and his minions decides is the public convenience? Ontario Hydro, Hydro-Quebec, the New Brunswick hydro utility company, the Canadian Petroleum Association and the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada all said this was a terrible provision. Showing how responsive it was, the Liberal Government of Canada amended that provision to read:

June 10, 1982
National Energy Board Act (No. 3)
-in the case of a licence, other than a licence for the exportation of power, the Board is of the opinion that the public convenience and necessity so requires.
The government exempted electrical power. On the one hand that, frankly, is an example of a responsive government. It is an example of another success as a result of the bellringing incident. If we had not had separate bills and opportunities for these utilities to make their views known in the committees, we would not have this improvement, which certainly is an improvement for electrical utilities. However, on the other hand, it is offensive, because it does not exclude natural gas. For goodness' sake, why in blazes can this government not be as responsive to the concerns of western Canadian gas producers as it is to central Canadian electricity producers? That is not to criticize the government for being responsive to the power utilities. That is an example of good government, but if we are to keep this blooming country together, and if this government is to be a national government for the whole nation-all of it from Newfoundland to Vancouver Island-at some point in time it must start to be as concerned about the problems and concerns of natural gas producers in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan as it is about electricity producers in Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick. We applaud the change but for goodness' sake why could the change not reflect the fact that this is the Government of Canada, all of Canada and not just central Canada or eastern Canada?
Clause 27 would allow the governor in council-again the minister and his minions-to set the prices for oil and gas exports. Again, how is the producer going to be able to negotiate an export sale of gas or oil when the governor in council can set the price? The United States has a deregulated oil and gas industry.

speechtext: Not gas yet. I am sorry. The minister is right, but oil is certainly deregulated, and soon gas will be. That means there is a marketplace. The price a producer can get for what he has to sell is the market price.

We will see. We will see. There is a marketplace. The price at which a commodity can be sold is the market price, so why in blazes put into law that the governor in council or the cabinet-the minister and his minions-will set the price? They might as well put it into law that the governor in council has the right to order that there shall be no rain on weekends. That would be a nice law and we would all approve, but the government is not capable of doing that. It is not capable of doing this either, but it can frighten potential buyers and make it more difficult for potential sellers. Of course, that is what the government is doing.
Clause 29 is even better in terms of big brother gone mad. This clause would set up a whole new part to the National
Energy Board Act which would give the National Energy Board the right to regulate all aspects of interprovincial oil and gas trade. Since 1980 and 1981 there have been various spokesmen for the government saying we have to change the Constitution of Canada so that we are at least a common market; if it is nothing else, Canada at least has to be a common market. No one argues about that. We should be a common market, but if we are a common market, then why in blazes do we have to have big brother regulating interprovincial trade in oil and gas through the National Energy Board? Is it trade when Saskatchewan Power buys gas from Alberta, or is that just persons in the same common market doing business with each other in the normal way? Is big brother going to treat Canada as some sort of collection of ten independent states which are to be regulated by the National Energy Board? Why is that in there? Why in blazes do we do that? The government will never admit it, but I think it has to do with federal-provincial conflicts. Big brother-the federal government-would like to have the legal authority to say to any province: "By cracky, if you want to sell your gas or your oil or if you want to buy some gas or oil, you are going to have to come through us." The federal government wants to control that. It wants to be in control of all aspects of interprovincial trade. That is offensive to my definition of Canada. That is offensive to any reasonable definition of Canada.
Hon. members opposite are getting a little bit impatient. I recognize that it is not their role to read and understand the legislation before they cast a vote. That would be an intolerable burden for backbenchers of the Liberal Party.
If I might be permitted an aside, Mr. Speaker, it is for that reason that we will probably never see electronic voting in this House so long as that party is in power. Could you imagine the chaos if hon. members opposite had to come up and vote electronically all by themselves without the example of their leader saying, "This is what to do; follow me."? They would have to think whether to vote for or against a particular motion. The situation would be chaotic if backbenchers opposite had to come here and listen to speeches now and again to know what is going on. That is, those who can read might have to do that.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that through the amendment the government brought in tonight-which was our amendment on second reading-calling for a six months' hoist it shows responsiveness by exempting electrical power from the cancellation of contracts on the basis of public convenience. However, by failing to show the same responsiveness to the concerns of oil and gas producers it has shown it is still not a Government of Canada in a complete sense, but a government of a very narrow part of Canada.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I want to correct a statement that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) made. He spoke about 25-year licences for the
June 10, 1982

export of oil. If he knew anything about the industry he would know that oil is sold on a monthly nomination basis and not by 25-year contracts. I keep trying to educate him. He is not in the House at the moment but I will keep trying and perhaps eventually he will learn a little bit about this part of our economy.
We will support the government's amendment, Mr. Speaker, and will look for a vote on our amendment. In total, although the bill is somewhat improved, it is still not sufficiently improved to justify our voting for it.
