subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-TASK FORCE REPORT ON PAYMENT OF GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES
PUBLIC WORKS-TASK FORCE REPORT ON PAYMENT OF GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, May 31 last, I directed a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove). If you remember, my question dealt with Bill C-4, the Municipal Grants Act, 1980.
In evidence brought before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, it had been suggested that the minister set up a task force whose reference would be to consider the key factors having an impact on municipal budgets, especially as far as the payment of grants in lieu of taxes was concerned. The minister had undertaken to submit to a task force the issue of the right of appeal in cases of differences of opinions on the real property assessment. In addition, an important matter, the use of the minister's discretionary power was to be considered by the task force chaired by Mr. Pollack. We know that in several clauses of Bill C-4, especially in Section 3, it is provided that the minister will have an absolute discretionary power. This, according to several witnesses heard before the committee, would give rise to some considerable problems with respect to municipal revenues.
Mr. Speaker, in almost all Canadian municipalities, we find several buildings for which the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) pays grants in lieu of taxes. It can be easily understood under the present circumstances that those municipalities whose budgets are more restricted are especially sensitive about that issue. For some of them, a relatively substantial part of their budget is based on those grants and it seems essential that a consultation or appeal process in case of differences of opinions be set up to provide them with some assistance.
Besides, we have seen this week, Mr. Speaker, that economic matters were the main concern of municipalities. Indeed, everyone knows that the Canadian Federation of Municipalities held its 45th convention right here in Ottawa and that the theme of the convention was precisely "The municipalities and the economy". Various economic themes were discussed during the convention, including the financial imputability of municipalities, the drawing up of municipal budgets, housing, employment and energy conservation as well as technological change.
That is why, considering the concerns of the municipalities, I asked the minister last week, before the convention was held, whether the task force had made its final report and whether
the minister would table or make public, before the convention in Ottawa this week, what seemed to me as being the rather significant findings of that report. The minister replied that indeed the task force had completed its work and that he was looking into the recommendations. Since then, he has said that the report will be made public in the near future.
As the committee has already completed its work, if the minister could table the report shortly, the participants to this convention would have been able to read this report and return to their respective regions to study its content. Since the representations made by the municipalities to the Pollack committee dealt with increased consultation in the decisionmaking process on matters concerning them, I suggest the minister would be well advised to let them express their views on the final recommendations of the task force before they are implemented. That is why I urge the minister to make public this report which is of tremendous importance for municipalities as soon as possible. This would contribute to a healthy dialogue between the parties and result in a happy agreement between the federal government and the municipalities concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Henri Tousignant (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-TASK FORCE REPORT ON PAYMENT OF GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES IN LIEU OF TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I shall, if I may, congratulate my hon. colleague from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) on his foresight in raising this very important matter of grants in lieu of taxes. I shall now take this opportunity to provide a detailed answer to the question he put on May 31.
During the hearings held by the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works early in 1980, before the new Municipal Grants Act was passed, many representatives from the provinces, municipalities and various associations submitted briefs criticizing the absence of an appeal procedure-as the hon. member mentioned-which would make it possible to resolve differences of opinion, and also the minister's discretionary powers. At his suggestion, the minister set up a task force that would analyse the situation and submit a report to the minister. The task force, chaired by Mr. Isidore Pollack of Quebec City, had a work plan which included the following elements: a documentary research program on key factors affecting grants to municipalities, the development of various possible appeal procedures, an intensive program of field trips including meetings with recipients of grants and evaluating authorities, and finally, the drafting of a report to be submitted.
I have been informed that the task force has completed its mission and will submit its final report to the minister within the next few days. As the minister noted in the House on May 31, he will make this report available to members of the Standing Committee in due time. However, I can say at once
June 10, 1982

that this report will probably recommend, subject to certain provincial mechanisms, the setting up of some type of a review board to which the recipients of grants, including municipalities, will be able to submit their case. This board will then make recommendations to the minister.
According to information available to me, the Pollack Report will be substantial. I have to hurry, Mr. Speaker, since it is getting late. This report will deal with this issue and other related matters in detail and will provide all the facts, all the motives and every possible alternative. As I have already mentioned, this report will be made available to the members of the Standing Committee, where it can be the subject of an in-depth examination. In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that in my opinion, this is an excellent initiative on the part of the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), and I am convinced that the speedy action taken by our Department will meet with his approval.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: INDUSTRY-QUALITY OF RAILS PRODUCED BY SYDNEY STEEL CORPORATION. (B) IMPORTATION OF RAILS
INDUSTRY-QUALITY OF RAILS PRODUCED BY SYDNEY STEEL CORPORATION. (B) IMPORTATION OF RAILS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sometimes it is very difficult to get any degree of accurate information around this place concerning matters involving transport. We have seen this with respect to Mirabel and with respect to a number of issues, but the one I wish to discuss tonight is the situation involving orders for the Sydney Steel Corporation in Sydney, Nova Scotia.
On May 11, I attempted to raise some questions in the House. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in his usual way, seemed to, as Allan Fotheringham would say, "fuzzify the modification". First, the minister said quite clearly that there was a problem with Sydney Steel as far as the quality of the rails was concerned. When outside of the House he said that, of course it was a mistake. There was nothing wrong with the rails. What has happened recently is that the people of Cape Breton and Nova Scotia are getting terribly concerned at what precisely is going on for the future of this vital regional industry. It is quite clear there is a certain amount of responsibility upon the government, whether it is on the basis of regional industrial expansion or whether it is on the basis of simply good transportation policy, to make certain that an institution, which is what Sydney Steel is, that over the years has received so much help and assistance from various political parties and levels of government is maintained in a reasonable way so that the 2,000 people who reside in that area can continue to earn a decent living.
The impression has been given, whether rightly or wrongly, by certain members and by the minister that indeed the matter is under control and that there is an order imminent for SYSCO from the CNR. I learned, much to my shock today, in the Standing Committee on Transport when I had a chance to speak and question directly the chief executive officer of the CNR, that, despite the impression that has been left in certain quarters, the Minister of Transport has not, and I repeat, has not in any way given a direct order or a directive to tell CNR
Adjournment Debate
to buy any amount of rails whatsoever from Sydney Steel. I think it is time this was clearly put on the record, and that is why I am doing this tonight.
In answer to his own colleague on June 7, 1982, the minister indicated, in his own inimitable style, that a contract is a contract is a contract. It reminds me of some of the statements he made about Mirabel. He cannot make a decision there either. The problem is that he wants to be all things to all people. He is sort of a parliamentary push me-pull me. He wants everyone to love him and to think he is great, but he never makes a decision. As far as Sydney, Nova Scotia, is concerned, there are many people-municipal leaders and ordinary working people-who are tired of misinformation. On June 7 he said that a contract is a contract is a contract, but that having made a commitment he was willing to press CN to honour it.
I found out in the Standing Committee on Transport today that he has not done a damn thing. He has not said a word to top management of CN. CN used to advertise itself as a business as well as a responsibility. I have no quarrel with that at all. If CN wants to run a hard-nosed business operation, that is fine. But it is a Crown corporation, it is ostensibly owned by the people of Canada, and it is controlled by the government. The Minister of Transport has the authority, as Dr. LeClair conceded today, to order CN to do something, and CN will do it.
The point is that the minister has not yet done a damn thing as I said, and an impression has been created in the House and in the province of Nova Scotia that something is being done. I fail to see why in the past it was necessary to import rail from outside of Canada when Sydney Steel Corporation had the capacity to do it. I fail to see why at the present time it is urgent that about 50,000 tonnes of rail be ordered from Algoma. I cannot understand that either.
I cannot understand why there is not some co-ordination between the Department of Transport and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce or the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, or whatever is the amalgam of these two hybrids now that we are rid of DREE. I cannot understand why the government will not take some step or why there is no co-ordination. I remember when a former minister of transport, now the distinguished Speaker in the other place, used to get headlines from time to time by saying, "Transportation is a component of regional development." Now we have a situation where a Crown corporation, which is receiving about $100 million in aid from the federal government, is being hung out to dry because the government would not spend $1.4 million and use its influence to ensure that some rails are purchased from that corporation.
Some $1.3 billion has been guaranteed to Canadair by the government to take the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce off the hook and so Russ Harrison can sleep nights; some $400 million is involved in a subsidy to Bombardier so that it can

June 10, 1982
Adjournment Debate
make railway cars to export, and that is fine with me; about $400 or $500 million is guaranteed to Massey-Ferguson, that great non-winner; but it is not possible for the Minister of Transport to make available $1.4 million, to use a figure which the minister himself used in the House of Commons, to guarantee the survival of about 2,000 people in Cape Breton, their jobs and their livelihoods.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: INDUSTRY-QUALITY OF RAILS PRODUCED BY SYDNEY STEEL CORPORATION. (B) IMPORTATION OF RAILS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just last Saturday 1 personally visited Sydney and, therefore, I know how important this issue is to the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) and his constituents.
Indeed the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) made reference at the time of the hon. member's question to problems encountered by CN with respect to the capabilities of Sydney Steel Corporation to produce rail which would meet the requirements of CN. But the hon. member was present at the meeting of the Standing Committee on Transport where he heard from the CN president himself who confirmed that yes, there is a contract for 88,000 tonnes of steel. But he did make it very clear that in that contract is included soft rail, hard 136 rail and the alloy type of rail.
There have been discussions between CN and Sysco on this matter as recently as today. These discussions are continuing. We all hope that the problem can be satisfactorily resolved. 1 am also pleased to report on behalf of the minister that the government of Nova Scotia has agreed, by a telex yesterday, to meet the federal government's offer to pay half of the $1.4 million cost of advancing the 1982-83 rail order by two months ahead of the time when the shipment would normally be required by CN. 1 think that this is welcome news.
I would also like to indicate to the House that, as confirmed yesterday in the other place, workers who were laid off at the SYSCO plant, will, indeed, receive unemployment insurance benefits in accordance with applicable regulations.
I thank the hon. member for Central Nova for giving me the opportunity of bringing the House up to date on this important issue. I commend him, as well as the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), and the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) for their constant interest and intervention in this matter.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: ACQUISITION OF PETROFINA-COLLECTION OF TAX-(B) CANADIAN OWNERSHIPCHARGE
ACQUISITION OF PETROFINA-COLLECTION OF TAX-(B) CANADIAN OWNERSHIPCHARGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 27 I received a letter from Mr. Reynolds of Surrey. He says the following:
You may not have had time to look at your persona! hydro bills over the past nine or ten months, but they must be similar to mine as we both live in Surrey, although I do pay my hydro bills on an equal payment installation to spread the load and you may not.
Please peruse the attached copies of three of my hydro bills from June 81 to April 82 ("June, $45.00, September $66.00 and now May will be $72.00, a 50
per cent increase in ten months"), whereas, my annual negotiated settlement ranges from 8 per cent to 12 per cent last year, over the past few years.
My hydro bills may be low compared to some, but I have spent considerable monies on insulation and doublepane windows and 1 do not qualify for CHIP.
This hydro bill, along with the telephone increase, the car/gas increase which is ridiculous and the general increase in all items especially food is beginning to break the camel's back. What you can do about it, I don't know but someone has got to do something pretty soon.
The taxes he is referring to are the federal excise tax and the Canadian ownership tax. The first problem with the Canadian ownership lax is the accumulated squeeze of human misery that that tax, along with other federal taxes, is weighing down on the Canadian taxpayers.
It is because of that letter and others like that, and remarks made in the House on the evening of May 16 by one of the government backbenchers regarding the Canadian ownership charge, that I raised the questions on May 17 with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). At that time I asked:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Last Thursday, here in the House, the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex indicated that while the government is collecting the Canadian ownership charge to pay for Petrofina, it might well continue to collect that tax even after Petrofina has been paid for. Could the minister tell the House if that is indeed government policy to collect that tax after Petrofina has been paid for in order to pay the purchase of other companies it wants to take over, as the hon. member suggested might be the case?
That was the question. The minister's reply was:
-that is obviously a question which the government will have to decide when the time comes.
This is not a matter which is being considered at the present time.
We do have some slightly contradictory statements between that of the backbencher, who is a former parliamentary secretary, and that of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. What is common to the two answers, however, is the fact that the government is not ruling out the possibility that the Canadian ownership charge could well be collected beyond the time which the government has paid for Petrofina in full. It does remind one of that temporary tax which was placed on the backs of Canadians during the First World War. It was known as the income tax, which was also a temporary tax. All of us know how temporary that is.
It is that accumulation of taxes which loads on to the backs of Canadians the kind of human misery that is killing them. When the takeover of Petrofina was announced, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that the purchase may have to be made by the Canadian ownership charge, but no figures were given. Mr. Hopper of Petro-Canada said the whole deal would be financed out of taxes. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources also said that the deal would be financed over 25 months. But when the company is paid for, the average energy consumer will have paid $130, and all of those dollars will have flooded the country and have gone back overseas to Europe. They will have done nothing for Canadian self-sufficiency, they will have done nothing to increase our energy security, but they will have continued to increase the taxes on the backs of Canadians.
June 10, 1982

The second part that is offensive about all of this taxation is that the government has no mandate for it. All of us clearly remember the election campaign of 1979-80 when the Liberals strenuously campaigned on the commitment that they would not increase taxes on gasoline by more than 12 cents or 14 cents, and certainly under 18 cents. The Canadian ownership charge increases the tax on that alone by 4.5 cents per gallon of gas, and the total has been something like 60 cents already.
1 find it repugnant that the government will campaign on one issue and then assume that the elections it has won on that one issue gives it a mandate to lead in any direction that it wants to lead.
The third problem rises out of the question that I placed before the minister. What are the government's intentions with regard to the future of the Canadian ownership tax which is being loaded on to the back of the consumer for a very sterile investment? What is the future of that? The minister has not been clear in the House as to his intentions. Is he planning to continue that tax beyond next fall when Petrofina will be paid for? Will he continue collecting that tax? Can we have an assurance tonight that when Petrofina is paid for, the Canadian taxpayers will not be saddled with a continuation of that particular tax in order to make up a shortfall incurred and caused by deficiencies in other departments, but, rather, that that tax will be taken off so that there can be some relief for the Canadian taxpayer? Does the parliamentary secretary have an answer for my constituents tonight, and all other Canadians who are incensed at the imposition of a tax for which the government had absolutely no mandate?

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ACQUISITION OF PETROFINA-COLLECTION OF TAX-(B) CANADIAN OWNERSHIPCHARGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is nice to be able to conclude this evening with a few remarks in answer to the questions raised by the hon. member. The first part of the hon. member's question, relative to the continued collection of the Canadian ownership charge in order to finance new acquisitions once Petrofina has been paid for, is obviously one which cannot be answered at the present time. When initially responding to this question during the question period, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) stated, "The government is not currently considering such
Adjournment Debate
policy and it is a matter which will have to be dealt with at the appropriate time".
With reference to the second part of the question as to whether we can afford to Canadianize the oil and gas industry,
I think the question ought to be rephrased and should read, "Can we afford not to Canadianize the oil and gas industry?" That is the substantive and, indeed, crucial question.
May I take a moment, Mr. Speaker, to remind the hon. member of the Canadianization goals as defined in the National Energy Program. One of the goals is an increase in the oil and gas sector owned by the Government of Canada. The National Energy Program also says that the Government of Canada intends to acquire several of the large oil and gas firms. To finance a company acquisition, a special charge, which the hon. member has referred to, the Canadian ownership special charge, is levied on all oil and gas consumption in Canada. The proceeds of this charge are placed to the Canadian ownership account, which is a non-budgetary trust account.
I might add that this particular piece of legislation was thoroughly reviewed before the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation, when Members of Parliament from all parties had an opportunity to question the government and the officials as to the intent of that particular account.
The Canadian Ownership Account was designed to ensure that the government's program of increasing public sector ownership would be self-financing. By imposing the Canadian ownership special charge as a means of financing public acquisitions, there is no drain on the general revenue fund. Canadians, the beneficiairies of the acquisition program, will be paying for the acquisitions through a special tax on their oil and gas purchases. The Canadian ownership account has already been used by the Government of Canada to finance the Petrofina acquisition.
I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by reiterating that the government is not in a position at this time to state very clearly whether or not further acquisitions will be made.
